# [3] https://rumbomundo.com/best-time-to-visit-iceland

The short answer: **July and August are the best months for most visitors.** But I have to warn you: no season is perfect for everything. You will have to give something up — at least for your first couple of trips.

**I’ve been to Iceland 9 times** over the past 7 years — all private trips — and I’m planning trip #10 this summer. Let me walk you through **the pros and cons of each season**.

In this article:

1. Why there’s no single best time to visit Iceland
2. What is the weather like in Iceland
3. Best time to visit Iceland — season overview
4. Summer (June–August): best for most visitors
5. Spring (April–May): best value
6. Autumn (September–October): proceed with caution
7. Winter (November–March): Northern Lights and solitude
8. Planning your trip — which guide is right for you?
9. A Few Things Iceland Won’t Warn You About

## There’s no single best time to visit Iceland

Every season in Iceland is genuinely worth it — for specific things. Summer brings relative warmth, up to 23 hours of daylight, full access to the interior highlands, whales, and puffins.

From my personal experience **winter is highly underrated**: it gives you **the Northern Lights and the spectacular ice caves** inside Vatnajökull glacier — both far more spectacular in person than any photo suggests. Plus snow-covered landscapes that summer visitors simply never see.

Spring offers long days at meaningfully lower prices. And Autumn is the odd one out — in my view the **low prices are its only real advantage**.

So when is the best time to visit Iceland? It depends on **what matters most to you**. Here’s how to decide:

* ### Want to see it all, but go only once?

  ![Chart of the best time to visit Iceland month by month — weather, daylight, prices, northern lights, puffins, whales, ice caves and more](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/best-time-to-visit-iceland-month-by-month-chart-150x150.png)

  When to go to Iceland

  Sorry my friend, no can do, you’re out of luck. **Seeing everything in one go is just not possible with Iceland**. Midnight Sun, puffins, and the interior highlands are **summer-only**, while Northern Lights and ice caves are **winter-only**. These are just some examples and there’s no workaround. **You need to visit at least twice** – happens to many a visitor 🙂 See the table **below** for all the details.
* ### Want to see as much as possible in one go?

  ![Group of hikers on the Fimmvörðuháls trail with a sweeping panorama of the Iceland highlands in the background](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/fimmvorduhals-9953-150x150.jpg)

  Fimmvörðuháls trail

  Go for a **summer trip, with a 4×4 vehicle and at least 15 days** at your disposal. You get all the top spots on Ring Road, as well as the Westfjords, interior highlands, whales, puffins, Midnight Sun, a chance for a couple of amazing hikes and the best weather to top it all. It might be quite expensive, but **it will certainly be memorable**. See our 15-day self-drive guide for details.
* ### Best value for money?

  **May or September are probably your best options**. Near-summer daylight, meaningfully lower prices, manageable weather and the Ring Road largely to yourself. Our 7–13-day Ring Road guide fits perfectly.
* ### Travelling on a budget?

  ![Tent pitched at Bolungarvík campsite in the Westfjords on a sunny June day, with mountain view in the background.](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Bolungarvik-campsite-150x150.jpg)

  Bolungarvík, Westfjords

  Choose **June or September if you’re happy to camp** — both months work for tent travel at lower prices. Spring is **the smartest balance** of cost and conditions. Autumn is the cheapest, but the weather is a genuine gamble.  
  Consider also simply **keeping your trip short**: you can easily see 60–70% of Iceland’s top spots in under a week, and our 3–7-day guide works great as a budget option in any season.
* ### Northern Lights and ice caves your priority?

  ![Vivid spiral multicolour aurora borealis lighting up the sky over a road on Iceland's south shore](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/IMG_1371-1000-150x150.jpg)

  Winter Iceland

  Then you need to **face Iceland’s winter** — there is no alternative. Both of these are winter-only experiences. February and March offer the best combination of aurora activity and clearer skies. See our complete winter Iceland guide for everything you need to plan.

With this in mind this guide starts with a **weather reality check** — Iceland’s climate surprises most first-time visitors, and understanding it shapes everything that follows. Then let me walk you through each season in turn: what it genuinely delivers, what it costs, and what kind of trip it actually suits. If you’re interested in **details for each month** – be sure to see our Iceland weather guide, which shows temperatures, wind, precipitation and more, based on raw data from **Icelandic Meteorological Office, for years 2000-2025**.

Weather shows the average daily high (°C / °F), wind (m/s) and rainfall (mm) — Reykjavík, Icelandic Met Office 1996–2025. Wind can lower the felt temperature by 5–8°C. Winter tyres are mandatory 1 Nov–15 Apr; rentals come fitted with studded winter tyres (studs allowed only in that window — Samgöngustofa). Winter also brings storm and road-closure risk. Midges affect lakes and rivers nationwide on calm, warm days. Ice caves = natural blue-ice caves; man-made and Katla tunnels run year-round.

## What Is the Weather Like in Iceland?

Most of Iceland has a Subpolar Oceanic climate — which may sound mild, but is deceiving. Average temperatures are never extreme in either direction, yet individual days can swing far from those averages. A summer day in Reykjavik can be a pleasant 18°C in sunshine or a miserable 8°C in horizontal rain — sometimes both on the same day.

Ef **þér líkar ekki veðrið, bíddu í fimm mínútur** — if you don’t like the weather, wait five minutes (local saying). Iceland’s weather doesn’t just change day to day — it can swing from sunshine to horizontal rain and back within the hour. **Pack for everything, every single day** — summer being the one genuine exception.

A few things to understand before picking your season:

### Typical temperatures in Iceland

* around **4°C / 39°F in winter** with 92.3% of days falling between -2°C / 28°F and 10°C / 50°F max. daily temp.
* around **9°C / 48°F in spring and autumn** with 94.2% of days falling between 3°C / 37°F and 15°C / 59°F.
* around **14°C / 57°F in summer** with 92.7% of days falling between 9°C / 48°F and 19°C / 66°F.

All above is based on Icelandic Meteorological Office Database, delivery 2026/01/06  
See a more detailed review of Iceland’s weather in our Weather in Iceland guide.

**Iceland’s seasons bleed into each other** more than you’d expect. Averages shift by just 5°C/9°F from one season to the next, and any given day can easily run the same 5°C/9°F above or below that average. A warm spring day and a cool summer day are often the same temperature.

**Strong winds will make it feel much colder** than the actual temperature — sometimes dramatically so.

**Snow and icy roads are not unusual** from September through to May, especially in the northern parts of the island.

### Wind is Iceland’s defining feature

Icelandic wind can make a 10°C day feel genuinely miserable, and it never fully goes away. For many locals, “good weather” simply means not much wind. Windproof layers are non-negotiable. Always check weather alerts on vedur.is before heading out — they’re almost always wind-related.

### Rain is frequent, but uneven

Iceland splits fairly clearly into more rainy months and less rainy ones. April through August averages 9–13 days per month with meaningful rainfall; September through March climbs to 16–18 days — well over half the month.

In summer, it tends to arrive in short heavy bursts — dry stretches of 2–3 weeks are entirely normal. September sees roughly double the total precipitation of June, and the rain there is far more persistent.

In winter, rain often becomes sleet — that grim mix of rain and snow near 0°C — but it can change to heavy snow at any time. Autumn is the wettest and cloudiest season by a clear margin, spring the second most unsettled.

### Daylight swings are extreme.

In late June, Reykjavik gets about 23 hours of daylight. In late December, fewer than 5 — and those hours are often under heavy cloud cover, so the day gets no brighter than a dim grey. This shapes everything — from how long you can drive to what you can see, enjoy and photograph.

Want the full picture before you decide when to go and what to pack? Our **Iceland weather guide** goes much deeper — monthly temperature highs and lows, wind speeds, precipitation and snow, sunlight hours — all built on **actual data from Iceland’s Met Office, not guesswork**. Worth a read.

| Best time to visit Iceland — season overview | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Season | Months | Temp. | Daylight | Precip. | Windy days | Crowds | Prices |
| **Summer** | Jun–Aug | 13–15°C 55–60°F | 17–23 h | ~50 mm | ~2 days | High | High |
| **Spring** | Apr–May | 7–10°C 45–50°F | 14–20 h | ~60 mm | ~6 days | Med. | Med. |
| **Autumn** | Sep–Oct | 8–12°C 45–55°F | 10–16 h | ~90 mm | ~7 days | Low–Med | Low–Med |
| **Winter** | Nov–Mar | 3–5°C 37–41°F | 4–12 h | ~85 mm | ~10 days | Low | Low–Med |

***All figures:** seasonal averages for Reykjavik, 2000–2025.  
**Temp.:** average daily maximum temperature.  
**Daylight:** time between astronomical sunrise and sunset.  
**Windy days:** days per month with avg. wind speed ≥10 m/s (36 km/h).  
**Source:** Icelandic Meteorological Office 2026: Icelandic Meteorological Office Database, delivery 2026/01/06, IMO self service.*

The pattern is clear: **summer delivers the best conditions at the highest cost**; **winter flips that completely**. **Spring is the value window** — near-summer daylight at lower prices with far fewer people. Autumn is the one exception: the numbers look appealing, but the weather makes it the hardest season to recommend without caveats. Read on for the details.

## Summer (June–August): Best for Most Visitors

Summer is peak season for good reason. This is Iceland at its most accessible — **warmest temperatures**, the least rain, maximum daylight, and full access to every road on the island. The Midnight Sun — the sun staying above the horizon around midnight, from mid-June to mid-July — is a genuine experience. **June** actually has the longest days of the year, lower prices than July and August, and the north and east at their driest.

![a car crossing the river ford in Landmannalaugar, Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Landmannalaugar-brod-225x150.jpg)interior

![maskonur (puffin)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Latrabjarg-maskonur_9646-225x150.jpg)puffins

![camping at Basar Hut](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Basar-Hut-camping-IMG_0064-225x150.jpg)camping

![man near Kirkjufell, Iceland in summer](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/summer-day-august-225x150.jpg)warm days

What the temperature figures alone don’t show: summer also has **Iceland’s calmest wind** — typically just **2 seriously windy days per month**, compared to 7 in autumn and 10 in winter. With typical temperatures approaching **20°C (68°F)**, light wind and plenty of sunshine, Iceland often feels genuinely warm and comfortable.

**One caveat:** August is where conditions begin to turn — precipitation climbs noticeably and the season is already trending toward autumn well before the month ends, even as temperatures remain summer-like.

### Main pros and cons of visiting Iceland in summer

* **Warmest, driest weather** of the year.
* **Most F-roads open from around June 15th** — access to Landmannalaugar, Þórsmörk, Kerlingarfjoll, Askja and many more; always check current status at road.is before heading out.
* **Up to 23 hours of daylight** — drive and photograph at any hour you choose (but do **pack a sleeping mask** — this is not optional).
* All tourist services, campsites and mountain huts fully operational (most from **mid-June**) — and if you’re happy camping or travelling by campervan, summer is the only season where it’s genuinely comfortable; a **great way to cut accommodation costs** significantly.
* **Puffins in full season** throughout summer — peak numbers in June and July, still present through August.
* **Whale watching at its finest** – best enjoyed in summer months on the northern shores of Iceland. See details here: Whale Watching in Iceland – All You Need to Know [Complete Guide].

* Most expensive time of year — accommodation and car hire peak sharply in July.
* Popular spots can get busy — noticeably more visitors than other seasons.
* Accommodation for July and August **should be booked 6 months ahead minimum** — popular places fill fast, despite being expensive; guided tours are more flexible, but top day trips fill up too.
* No Northern Lights and natural glacier ice caves not accessible in summer.

### How to Plan a Summer Trip to Iceland

Summer is the most flexible season — **almost any kind of trip works here**. The holy grail is a full loop around the island, including the Westfjords, in a 4×4 with at least 14 days (ideally 20), including nights at highland campsites — this is the only season that makes it possible.

Summer is also the **only season for multi-day hiking** — Laugavegur, Fimmvörðuháls, Hellismannaleið, Hornstrandir and others are summer-only, and Iceland is one of the rare destinations where you can have a genuinely great trip without renting a car at all.

But summer also suits the **standard Ring Road drive** or a **short south-west trip** perfectly well; camping and campervans are a great budget option, though hotels and guesthouses are available if price isn’t your main concern.

See our 15-day summer guide for the full highland experience, or our 7–13 day Ring Road guide if you’re skipping the interior.

## Spring (April–May): Best Value

April and May are increasingly popular — and for good reason. Days grow long fast (**20 hours of daylight in May**), prices are **significantly lower than summer**, and the roads are quiet. The landscape turns vivid green after winter, and waterfalls are at their most powerful from snowmelt.

![approach to Skogafoss](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/skogafoss-2148775318430976-480x320.jpg)Skogafoss

![Dimmuborgir – the 'Black Fortress’ Lava Field](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Dimmuborgir_4810-1-480x320.jpg)Dimmuborgir

![Top 10 Things You Need to Do in Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/D71_8866-480x320.jpg)

![Reykjadalur](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Reykjadalur_1332-480x320.jpg)Reykjadalur

**May often already feels genuinely pleasant** — wind and rain ease off to near-summer levels, even if temperatures don’t quite catch up yet.

### Main pros and cons of visiting Iceland in spring

* **Significantly cheaper** than summer — car hire and accommodation often 30–50% lower than July.
* **Long days**: up to 20 hours of daylight in May.
* **Fewer crowds** — noticeably less busy than summer, though Iceland’s main attractions are never truly empty.
* **Puffins arrive** from late April — you can already meet them at their favourite spots.
* **Campervans are a great option** — many sites are open from early spring or year-round. Tent camping is possible, but challenging, especially in April; summer is the better call for tents.

* Weather is unpredictable — snow on mountain passes is still possible in April.
* Most highland F-roads remain closed until late June.
* April is notably windier than summer — around 6 seriously windy days per month versus 2 in summer; May drops off sharply.

### How to Plan a Spring Trip to Iceland

Spring is tailor-made for the **Ring Road** — **10–14 days** in a regular car, staying in hotels, hostels or guesthouses, which are well-priced and comfortable at this time of year.

Seven days works as a minimum if that’s all you have, though you’ll feel the time pressure. A shorter **3–7 day** south-west trip is also a solid option. Campervans work too, though **hostels are the more comfortable and practical choice** in unpredictable spring weather. See our 7–13 day Ring Road guide for details.

## Autumn (September–October): Proceed With Caution

Autumn is the **most difficult season to recommend unreservedly**. Yes, it’s the least expensive season (and significantly so), and some autumn days are genuinely beautiful — but more often than not, the weather is really bad.

**Rain, wind, and rapidly shortening days** define the season. Iceland has a word for the deceptive autumn sky: ***gluggaveður* — window weather** — meaning it’s best to enjoy through the glass. The ability to dry your clothes overnight often becomes your main concern.

![Couple looking at Skógafoss waterfall on a sunny autumn day in Iceland, with a rainbow formed in the mist and clear blue sky above](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/skogafoss-waterfall-rainbow-sunny-autumn-iceland-480x320.jpg)Skógafoss, October

![Author standing on Diamond Beach Iceland in horizontal rain, soaked jacket, grey skies and waterlogged parking lot behind](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/diamond-beach-iceland-autumn-rain-typical-weather-480x320.jpg)Diamond Beach, October

![Shoe rack with electric shoe dryer at Midgard Basecamp hostel entrance, with wet hiking boots drying](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/midgard-basecamp-hostel-shoe-dryer-iceland-480x360.jpg)Hit machine

![Worn paper sign on a wall radiator in Vík Iceland reading "please don't use the radiator to dry clothes"](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/vik-iceland-radiator-no-drying-clothes-sign-480x320.jpg)The eternal struggle

The crossing to “wet season” begins in **late August** — and by September it’s unmistakable: from around **10 rainy days in July to 16 in September and beyond**, from **49 mm of precipitation to 96 mm**, and average wind picking back up from **11 to 14 km/h**.

**Autumn is the season to choose** if summer prices are out of reach but you still want to see the country. Just make sure **waterproof means waterproof, head to toe**.

### Main pros and cons of visiting Iceland in autumn

* **Prices drop sharply** from summer peaks — October and November are **the most affordable months** in the calendar. If you’re willing to take a risk with the weather, autumn is Iceland on a genuine budget.
* **Northern Lights return from mid-September** — October offers solid viewing conditions (if the skies are clear).
* **Crowd levels drop significantly** from mid-September onward (but many campsites close for winter then).

* **Poor weather becomes the norm** — especially in the East and North of the country.
* September is still a bit busy: cruise ship season hasn’t fully ended, south coast spots remain crowded despite worsening conditions.
* Highland F-roads close progressively through September, some as early as mid-month.
* **Daylight drops fast:** from around 15–16 hours in early September to under 10 by late October.

### How to Plan an Autumn Trip to Iceland

Autumn works much like spring in terms of what’s possible — Ring Road or short south-west trip, regular car, similar trip lengths. The key difference is accommodation: **hostels are strongly advisable** over camping or campervans. You’ll want a warm base, a drying rack, and a hot shower after most days out. See our 7–13 day Ring Road guide for more details and recommended itinerary.

## Winter (November–March): Northern Lights and Solitude

Winter in Iceland is demanding, but it delivers things that simply don’t exist at any other time of year: Northern Lights, natural ice caves, extraordinary glacial landscapes, and (usually) **affordable prices**. Once the New Year has passed, the days are lengthening, high-pressure systems bring clearer skies, and the Northern Lights are much easier to catch as a result.

![Vivid spiral multicolour aurora borealis lighting up the sky over a road on Iceland's south shore](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/IMG_1371-1000-225x150.jpg)Aurora in the south

![Person standing inside a beautifully lit blue ice cave tunnel in Vatnajökull glacier near Jökulsárlón, Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/jaskinia-lodowa-8-225x150.jpg)Vatnajökull ice cave

![Person examining a naturally fish-shaped piece of glacial ice on Diamond Beach Iceland, sunlight shining through the ice with sparkling reflections, ocean in the background](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/diamond-beach-iceland-winter-natural-ice-sculpture-sunlight-225x150.jpg)Diamond Beach, winter

![Bird's eye view of a white car on the snow-covered Ring Road (Route 1) surrounded by white winter landscape in Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/DJI_0180-zima-225x150.jpg)Ring Road, winter

On the temperature front, **the cold itself is often more manageable** than you might expect. In December, only about 1 day in 7 (13.6%) sees the maximum temperature stay below freezing, while more than a third (42%) of **December days enjoy 6°C / 43°F or higher**. Nights of course do feel wintry, but only a third of them fall below -5°C / 23°F. See the histograms below for details.

![Bar chart of daytime high temperatures distribution in Iceland in winter (November–March), Reykjavik 2000–2025, in degrees Celsius. Most days fall between -5°C and 10°C](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-winter-daytime-high-temperatures-350x350.jpg)Daytime highs

![Bar chart of overnight low temperatures at ground level in Iceland in winter (November–March), Reykjavik 2000–2025, in degrees Celsius. Most nights fall between −10°C and 5°C](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-winter-overnight-low-temperatures-350x350.jpg)Overnight lows

Daily maximum temperatures stay **above 0°C / 32°F in every winter month** (statistically, averaged, for years 2000-2025). *Source: Icelandic Meteorological Office 2026: Icelandic Meteorological Office Database, delivery 2026/01/06, IMO self service*

Of course Iceland’s weather is all about crazy changes, so these **averages can be misleading**. You should not be surprised if the daily highs on your specific winter trip range anywhere from −10°C (14°F) to +10°C (50°F). **Wind is a bigger challenge** in Iceland’s winter.

**Wind is the most dangerous driving factor in winter Iceland — not ice or snow.** Studded tyres handle slippery roads well as long as you slow down; wind strong enough to push a car off the road is a different matter entirely. **Check wind alerts on vedur.is before every journey** and avoid driving under orange or red weather alerts. Pay at least as much attention to the wind forecast as to road conditions.

In eastern and northern Iceland you’ll find high mountain passes on the Ring Road that are often temporarily closed in winter — either due to heavy snow and ice, or extreme winds. Therefore choosing **to drive all around Iceland in winter is a high-risk decision**.

### Main pros and cons of visiting Iceland in winter

* **Northern Lights** — the window runs October through April, but **February and March** typically offer the best combination of clear skies and dark nights.
* **Natural ice caves** inside Vatnajökull glacier — also best enjoyed in February and March.
* **Affordable prices** — car hire and accommodation often **40–60% below July rates**.
* Iconic spots (Seljalandsfoss, Skógafoss, Jökulsárlón) — often **near-empty**.
* Dramatic snow-covered landscapes unlike anything summer offers.

* All highland F-roads completely closed and mountain sections of the Ring Road can close temporarily too (esp. in East and North).
* Very limited daylight: **4–6 hours in December and January**.
* Severe storms significantly more frequent than in other seasons

### How to Plan a Winter Trip to Iceland

Winter works best as a focused short trip — **around 5 days is the sweet spot**, and there’s little reason to push beyond that. Stay on the **South and West shores**, don’t attempt the full Ring Road, and **book yourself into hotels or guesthouses**.

Check weather alerts on **vedur.is** before every journey — in winter Iceland, a storm can change everything within hours. The rewards — Northern Lights, ice caves, empty landscapes — are worth every constraint. See our 3–7 day guide and the complete winter Iceland guide.

## Planning Your Trip — Which Guide Is Right for You?

**Going all out in summer — 15-day 4×4 guide.** The full Iceland experience: Ring Road, Westfjords, highland F-roads, and everything in between. Needs at least 14 days, a 4×4, and some nights under canvas.

![Road sign on Iceland's highland interior route warning no gas station for the next 243 km](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/iceland-highland-road-no-gas-243km-sign.jpeg)

The Best 15-day Summer 4×4 Self Drive Plan for Iceland

**Spring, summer or autumn loop — 7–13 day Ring Road guide.** The standard Iceland trip done properly. Regular car, flexible trip length, works in any non-winter season.

![Collage of Iceland Ring Road highlights: lava eruption, Skógafoss waterfall, Icelandic horse portrait, and glacial lagoon](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-ring-road-highlights-volcano-skogafoss-horse-glacial-lagoon-705x307.jpeg)

Around Iceland – a 7 to 13-day Itinerary for Spring to Autumn

**Short trip or first-timer — 3–7 day south-west guide.** The essential Iceland highlights in under a week. The default choice for winter, and a solid option any time of year. Can also be done entirely without a car — great for solo travellers or pairs who’d rather not drive, and often cheaper for small groups.

![Collage of Iceland south-west highlights: Strokkur geyser erupting, Búðakirkja black church, ice block on Diamond Beach, and Blue Lagoon hot pool](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-southwest-highlights-strokkur-budakirkja-diamond-beach-blue-lagoon-705x307.jpeg)

SW Iceland’s greatest hits — a 3 to 7 Days Self Drive Itinerary

**Visiting Iceland without renting a car**: Sightseeing in Iceland without a car. Bus tours, cycling, hitchhiking, on foot — there are more options than most people realise, and they suit very different budgets and travel styles. Summer also opens up multi-day hiking trails: Laugavegur, Fimmvörðuháls, Hellismannaleið, Hornstrandir — among the best in the world. No vehicle needed, and a completely different Iceland from what most visitors see.

![Yellow tent pitched in Iceland's highland interior on an overcast day, surrounded by grass, marsh and volcanic sand](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-highland-tent-laugavegur-trail-interior-vista-705x306.jpeg)

Sightseeing in Iceland without a car – what are your options

**Winter specifically — complete winter Iceland guide.** Everything you need to know about planning a winter trip: Northern Lights, ice caves, where to stay, what to expect. Read this alongside whichever trip-length guide fits.

![White car driving on a snow-covered Ring Road through a completely white winter landscape in Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/iceland-winter-driving-ring-road-snow-white-landscape-705x306.jpeg)

Winter trip to Iceland – a Complete Guide

## A Few Things Iceland Won’t Warn You About

### How early should I book for Iceland?

**For out-of-season travel:**  
book your car (or camper) 2–3 months ahead; accommodation can generally be left to last minute.

**For high season**:  
book accommodation 3–6 months ahead, car rental 2–3 months. Individual tours can generally be booked later — most offer free cancellation up to 48 hours in advance, so there’s no harm in booking early. Some tours do sell out well ahead (popular ice cave time slots, for instance) — book those 1–2 months in advance. Browse a great catalogue of Iceland day tours and multi-day tours at rumbomundo.tourdesk.is.

**Booking campsites**:  
as a general rule, **campsites don’t require advance booking** — and most don’t even allow it. If you want an electric hook-up, call your preferred site 1–2 days ahead and ask them to keep one for you (where available). Two highland campsites are exceptions: Landmannalaugar (must be booked in advance; no electricity available) and Kerlingarfjöll — bookings are mandatory, and powered pitches must be selected at the time of booking; you can’t add electricity after the fact.

### What to pack for Iceland?

The essentials are windproof layers and a swimsuit — but Iceland adds a few items to the packing list that many travellers don’t anticipate:

* **swimsuit**, flip-flops, towel — visiting hot pools is **essential Icelandic experience** in every season. Some pools — the Blue Lagoon especially — have highly mineralised water that can be harsh on hair; **a shower cap, beanie, or hair tie** is worth packing if you care about that. You can also buy or rent shower caps at the pools.
* **water shoes** — useful in wild hot pools and essential on interior hikes (crossing streams).
* **sleeping mask** if you’re used to sleeping in darkness (so esp. if you travel in summer).
* **sunscreen** if you travel in summer – there’s no trees to hide from the 23-hour daylight.
* **insect repellent** if you travel in May-June; Iceland has small midges/gnats near lakes and rivers that can be bothersome (consider a **mosquito net hat**, if you’re allergic or hate getting swarmed).
* **windproof and waterproof outer layers** – if you hike trails like Laugavegur, you need top-notch protection; if you travel by car, you’ll be fine with “consumer-grade” gear (that is: unless you travel in Autumn and aim to sightsee no matter the weather).
* **Iceland map on your phone for offline use** – Google Maps lets you download the entire country to your phone and it’s the best way to navigate the island, especially where signal is poor. For hiking, use map**y**.com instead (not map**s**.com — an easy one to mix up).

### Is Iceland good for families with kids?

Very much so. Hot pools, puffins, whale watching, and geysers all work brilliantly with children. The **Perlan museum** in Reykjavik is the best start for a family trip — plenty of interactive exhibits, a “real” ice cave inside the building, and panoramic views of the city. Highland F-roads are **less suitable for young children** (rough terrain, long distances from services), and some glacier hikes have minimum age requirements. For the Ring Road and the south shore, Iceland with kids works beautifully.

### How expensive is Iceland?

Iceland is one of Europe’s most expensive destinations — though significantly cheaper outside summer. Expect roughly $50–80 for a restaurant main course, $100–150+ per night for budget accommodation, and minimum $100/day for car hire in high season. Travelling in autumn or spring (October–November especially) typically costs **30–50% less**. See this guide for all the important details: Prices in Iceland: How Much Is Food, Fuel, Tours

### Do I need cash in Iceland? How do I pay?

Cash is almost never needed — Iceland is one of the world’s most cashless societies. **Contactless payment (Apple Pay, Google Pay) works in 99% of places**, from Reykjavik restaurants to remote petrol stations. If you’re heading into the interior, carry 1,000 ISK per person just in case. ATMs are rare, so don’t count on finding one when you need it.  
Two things worth checking before you leave home: make sure your **card isn’t blocked for international transactions**; and make sure you **know your PIN**. In Iceland — as across Europe — card purchases are confirmed by PIN or contactless, not by signature. If your card isn’t added to your phone’s wallet, your PIN is your backup. Not knowing it at a remote petrol station is a genuinely bad situation to be in.

### Do I need a local SIM card in Iceland?

**EU travellers don’t need one** — Iceland is covered by the roam like at home policy, and you won’t see a bump in your bill. Just check that you have enough GB on your contract (use Google Maps navigation in offline mode only, if you’re not sure you have enough);  
**Non-EU travellers** will likely want a local SIM for calls and data. If your phone supports eSIM technology, you should be able to purchase an Icelandic eSIM even before leaving on the trip and that’s usually the most hassle-free solution.  
Either way, you can **skip the in-car Wi-Fi** from the rental company — your phone’s hotspot usually does a better job and for no extra fee.

### Do I need a 4×4 in Iceland?

Only if you’re planning to drive the highland F-roads in summer (Landmannalaugar, Þórsmörk (Thorsmork), Sprengisandur) – **rental companies won’t allow 2WD vehicles on F-roads**. A 4×4 is also worth considering if you’d feel more comfortable on slippery winter roads. For the Ring Road trip outside winter a regular car is perfectly fine. Always check road.is before any journey. And see our Complete Guide on Renting a Car in Iceland for lots of first-hand tips and details.

### When can I see whales in Iceland?

April through October, with peak season June–August. Húsavík in the north is Iceland’s whale watching capital, but tours also run from Reykjavik and several other ports. See our complete whale watching guide for details on where, when and what to expect.

### What are the absolute must-sees in Iceland?

Iceland’s top highlights span **natural wonders, breathtaking landscapes, wildlife, and geothermal hot pools**. The experiences most visitors put at the top of their list: geysers (esp. Strokkur), waterfalls (Skógafoss, Seljalandsfoss, Glymur, Dettifoss), the Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon with the adjacent Diamond Beach, Reynisfjara black sand beach, lava and volcano caves, natural ice caves inside Vatnajökull, whale watching, puffins, and geothermal hot pools. In winter, the Northern Lights join that list. The Golden Circle — Þingvellir, Geysir, Gullfoss — is the classic first-day itinerary from Reykjavik. For a curated selection with practical tips, see our Top 10 things to do in Iceland.

### What Can You Enjoy in Iceland All Year Round?

Two things stand out — and both tend to surprise first-time visitors. The hot pools and the food scene.

* **Hot pools and swimming pools**  
  These are a **genuine part of Icelandic daily life**, not just a tourist attraction. The variety is remarkable: small neighbourhood pools where locals actually swim laps in a 10-metre pool before work; mid-sized geothermal pools that are genuinely lovely; giant destination spas like the Blue Lagoon; and an endless scatter of wild or near-wild hot pots across the island, some barely marked on a map. The smart move is to **try at least one from each category**. In our family travels, **a day in Iceland without a hot pool visit requires a formal explanation** — and it rarely happens twice. See our complete guide to Iceland’s hot pools, spas and swimming pools for the full picture.
* **The food scene**  
  Iceland is expensive — a main course can easily run $70 — but lamb and langoustines here are genuinely world-class, traditional dishes like **hákarl, gellur and svið** are things you won’t find anywhere else, and there’s a quietly exciting new scene on top: hot dogs reinvented in a dozen ways, mathöll food halls, a greenhouse restaurant that puts its own tomatoes into everything including the beer. Worth exploring even on a budget. See our Iceland for Foodies guide.

See more **questions answered** on our extensive FAQ page. Or ask your question below, in the comments – we aim to answer them on same day.

![Chart of the best time to visit Iceland month by month — weather, daylight, prices, northern lights, puffins, whales, ice caves and more](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/best-time-to-visit-iceland-month-by-month-chart.png)

When to go to Iceland, month by month — at a glance. Data: Icelandic Met Office, 1996–2025.

# [4] https://rumbomundo.com/iceland-trip-costs

Iceland is expensive so when you plan to visit here it is important to look at how to cut costs. This article outlines what drives these costs, how they change and what you can do to limit them.

In this article:

1. What determines the cost of your trip to Iceland
2. Limiting the cost of an Iceland trip
3. The cost of accommodation and car rental in Iceland
4. Prices of flights to Iceland
5. The cost of food in Iceland
6. The cost of tourist attractions in Iceland
7. Total costs of a trip to Iceland
8. Other guides

## What determines the cost of your trip to Iceland

The biggest factors to consider when you are planning your trip to Iceland are usually **flights, accommodation and car rental**. And the amount of these costs mostly depends on **the month you choose for your visit**. All over the world you pay much more in high season than in low season, however, in Iceland the difference can be especially striking.

The prices of nearly everything are lowest from November to April and highest in July and August. The difference between winter and summer months in, for instance, the prices of rental cars can be as much as three times! Given the fact that hiring a car is a big cost component anyway, having to pay triple is really huge. May and June (also September and October) are somewhere in between. You’ll see specific examples below.

Obviously, one needs to add food and admissions fees to various tourist attractions. These costs vary depending on your preferences and overall approach to the trip. But below we give you an overview of these costs and some recommendations as to what to skip and which places are worth the price.

Remember that as much as everything is cheaper out of season, not everything is available. Many campsites, B&Bs or restaurants only operate from spring to autumn. Nearly all mountain roads, and therefore the whole interior, are only open and available from late June till early September (Read more: Major roads in Iceland). And ice caves operate exclusively in winter. So as you see, the timing of your trip is key not only from the point of view of your expenses but also your itinerary.

## Limiting the cost of an Iceland trip

Iceland is an expensive destination and it’s not uncommon to think about limiting the trip costs. Of course a short trip will be less expensive than a long one, but then in a per-day view, it will likely be the most expensive one.

So what can you do to visit Iceland and enjoy it, but don’t spend a fortune?

Even before you read the whole article, you can easily assume that the cheapest way to travel around Iceland is by bicycle or on foot. Then you don’t need to rent a car and buy insurance or gas. Moreover, while cycling and hiking through Iceland you can camp almost anywhere, so your cost of accommodation goes down to nearly zero (nearly, because it makes sense to spend the night at a proper campsite every few days).

But a cycling or walking trip is not for everyone. It requires solid preparations, really good gear, and if you want to see the whole of Iceland, your stay will have to be much longer. Iceland is a wonderland for hiking and biking enthusiasts and as costs of this kind of a trip don’t change too much between seasons, it is absolutely worth planning it for the summer months.

However, for most tourists the best and most convenient way to see Iceland will be be car. The most important rules to follow while organizing your trip and keep the costs low are as follows:

* go in a group of 4-5 people and hire a regular 5-seat car (or a wagon);
* if you are not going to visit the interior, don’t bother with a 4×4;
* drive super carefully, but skip the full coverage car insurance;
* bring your own tents and camping gear with you;
* camp and cook for yourselves;
* avoid attractions and tours you have to pay for – use free alternatives;
* shop in Bonus or Kronan stores (or Netto if the others are not available);
* go in May or June (could be in April if you don’t intend to sleep in a tent);
* book flights, car and accommodation minimum 6 months prior;

If  
you don’t go on paid tours and attractions, the cost of a week-long trip can go as low as under 500 EUR per person (see below).

## The cost of accommodation and car rental in Iceland

Choosing a car and places to stay are interlinked because Iceland offers a very interesting option of campervans + campsites. When you hire a campervan, you pay more than for a regular car but you save on accommodation. Often the total cost is very similar. But with a campervan comes a lot of flexibility: you don’t need to book campsites in advance so you can change your itinerary depending on the weather or yhow your group feels.

**Camping with a tent is obviously the cheapest option.** However, in April and May it can be a real challenge. And many campsites are still closed in April. Temperatures at nights go down to 10 ºC / 50 ºF or less even in the summer months. So sleeping in a tent may be a good idea from June to August. But even then very strong, cold winds are the norm, so sleeping in a tent, unpacking and packing up your stuff can prove tough.

Campervans are naturally more pricey than your own tent but even a big motorhome costs roughly the same per person as staying in hostels. A campervan is less comfy than a B&B or hostel but it gives you incomparably more freedom and flexibility.

In practice, a big advantage of hiring a campervan is that you can make tea or snacks in it throughout the day with no extra cost. In a country where a hot dog at a gas station sets you back 4-5 euro, these snacks and lunches can add up to a surprisingly large amount…

The table below illustrates prices of car rental and accommodation in May (for 7 days). For more comparisons (like car rental prices in other months) go here What kind of car to hire in Iceland.

| The cost of car rental and accommodation (for 7 days in May) | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| car model | pax | accomodation type | total cost (car+accom.) | cost per person | >>>> scroll right for details >>>> | car rental (7 days) | gas (1500 km) | accomodation | total cost | cost per person |
| Kia Rio | 4 pax | campsites tent | $400 | $100 | >>> | 31,000 kr | 24,675 kr | 32,807 kr | 55,675 kr | 13,919 kr |
| Hyundai i10 | 2 pax | hostels | $990 | $495 | >>> | 27,000 kr | 21,150 kr | 90,323 kr | 138,473 kr | 69,236 kr |
| Kia Rio | 4 pax | hostels | $1,700 | $420 | >>> | 31,000 kr | 24,675 kr | 180,645 kr | 236,320 kr | 59,080 kr |
| Renault Trafic | 8 pax | campsites campervan | $3,750 | $465 | >>> | 130,000 kr | 31,725 kr | 361,290 kr | 523,015 kr | 65,377 kr |
| kampervan Berlingo | 2 pax | campsites campervan | $1,055 | $530 | >>> | 110,133 kr | 37,600 kr | 14,581 kr | 147,733 kr | 73,867 kr |
| campervan Renault Master | 4 pax | campsites campervan | $1,800 | $455 | >>> | 211,795 kr | 42,300 kr | 32,807 kr | 254,095 kr | 63,524 kr |
| Motorhome Lux | 6 pax | campsites motorhome | $2,770 | $460 | >>> | 317,692 kr | 70,500 kr | 47,388 kr | 388,192 kr | 64,699 kr |

Of course, as you can see, the cheapest option is to go in a group of 4 people, hire a rather small car with no 4×4 function and sleep in a tent. This way the cost of your trip (excluding plane tickets, food and additional attractions) can be much lower than 250 eur per person. Other options take it up to about 500 eur per person.

As we said before, the price of car rental changes significantly between different months. Fore more comparisons and detailed tables as well as tips concerning what is worth vs. not worth doing read this article What kind of car to hire in Iceland. Below, we only show a couple of examples from that article.

| Cost of car rental in Iceland | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Toyota Aygo (2 pax) | Dacia Duster 4×4 (4 pax) | Renault Trafic (8 pax) | Campervan R. Master (5 pax) | Motorhome Luxury (6 pax) |
| April | $190 | $270 | $750 | $1,500 | $2,400 |
| June | $580 | $800 | $1,400 | $2,800 | $3,100 |
| July | $750 | $1,000 | $3,000 | $3,500 | $4,150 |
Examples of car rental prices in Iceland for 7 days.

As you can see, altough the change in price between April and June is huge, the summer prices are still significantly higher.

In July both campervans and motorhomes are twice as expensive as in April. But when you compare their prices to the cost of hiring a regular passenger car do not forget to take into account the cost of accommodation. If you don’t want to sleep in a tent the costs of accommodation will eat big part (if not all) of the price difference between these types of vehicles.

R  
egular car rental in July can be as much as 4 times more expensive than pre-season! If you don’t intend to visit the interior, then going to Iceland in summer is a true luxury.

Naturally, costs per person are to a large degree determined by the number of people traveling in the car. Campervan Renault Master with 4 people (and not 5 as calculated above) will be pricier per person than the luxury and spacious 6-person motorhome divided by 6.

Similarly, Toyota Aygo will clearly be the cheapest per person as long as it travels with 4 persons. However, you need to remember that having 4 people in a car this small means you need to have very little baggage. In practice, it is more of a 2-person car.

Interestingly, large, passenger vans do not cost less than regular cars. They become competitive per person compared to 4-person cars only when you divide the price into 9 people. But 9 people means 9 sets of baggage, which can be difficult to fit even in a big trunk of a van, especially if you take tents and camping gear.

P  
rices in the table assume hiring a car without additional insurance. Not all rental shops allow this and a full “platinum” package can **double the rental cost!**

Big motorhomes are an exception: They can’t be hired without a full or nearly full insurance package (so the prices above include insurance). This topic is discussed in more detail in a separate article – Car insurance in Iceland.

## Prices of flights to Iceland

Flight prices will depend so much on where are you flying from, that we can’t really discuss it here.

So let us just remind you that in low season one can buy plane tickets for half (or less) of the high season price.

Generally t is crucial to be flexible about flight dates because sometimes changing the departure or arrival date by a single day can save you hundreds of euros (or dollars)!

If  
you’re planning a winter trip, do make sure to put extra flexibility in your plans. On one hand you might get stuck on your way for a day or two because of bad weather, but on the other: your flight in (or out) might be delayed be days, rather than mere hours, because of bad weather. Be super flexible in your planning.

![Czytelny kalendarz niskich cen](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/july-skyscanner-en.jpg)

Low prices calendar

One of the best tools for finding cheap flights is Skyscanner. It quite clearly shows the lowest flight prices for the entire month. If we have the flexibility to choose the exact departure dates, we can select flights that are clearly cheaper than others. Even postponing the departure or return by one day, can strongly change the cost of tickets.

You can also take a ferry to Iceland and bring your own car with you. On long trips (about a month-long and longer) this could be an appealing alternative, if you can get to Denmark easily. The basic cost for 5 people and one regular passenger car with couchettes/bunk beds and no meals included is about 2700 EUR, about 550 EUR per person. This only route is operated by Smyril Line from the Danish port of Hirtshals.

## The cost of food in Iceland

If you cook for yourself and shop in supermarkets the costs of food should be about the same for you, as anywhere else in Europe.

12-13 EUR per person per day is a good estimate, although one can spend way more or a little bit less.

If you choose to eat out however, paying less than 25 euro / $30 per person will be a challenge.

![A gas station hot dog](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/islandzki-hotdog-150x150.jpg)

A gas station hot dog

This is something you need to remember if you are thinking of staying in B&Bs or hotels. If you can’t prepare your meals yourselves and have to rely on hotel restaurants and other such places along the way, your trip will become much more expensive. Bear in mind that just a hot dog at a gas station costs 4-5 euro!

Read more in these articles Grocery Shopping in Iceland: Prices and Store Opening Hours and Iceland for Foodies – What’s Worth Trying and Where.

## The cost of tourist attractions in Iceland

We presented a rather extensive list of top attractions with their prices and links to booking sites in the article Prices in Iceland: how much does food, fuel, attractions cost.

You visit most attractions on our own – for free and without a guide. Paid parking or admission to smaller attractions is a small cost – a total of $50 at most for the entire trip per person.

And a trip to Iceland is full of excitement even if you choose not to buy any of the guided trips, but still: some of them are really worth the price.

Below we present a list of attractions you should really include in your itinerary and a list of extras that you might go for, but they’re not really essential to understanding Iceland.

### Basic attractions

Basic attractions, the kind without which a trip to Iceland would be incomplete, are:

* **Visit an ice cave (or two)**  
  In winter, we recommend the caves near Jokulsarlon. And from spring to autumn: those in the Katla massif, near Vik. Everything you need to know about them can be found in this article: Icelandic ice caves – Iceland’s natural wonder.
* **Whale watching tour**  
  This is a bit expensive perhaps, but really worth the price, especially for animal lovers. Certainly most exciting in summer, as that’s when you’re least likely to get cold on the trip and most likely to see lots of large whales. A detailed article about all pros and cons waits for you here: Whale watching cruises in Iceland – how, where, when and for how much.
* **A visit to the Blue Lagoon**  
  The Blue Lagoon is certainly quite commercial, bustling and unfortunately expensive. And there’s great many alternatives to it in Iceland. But in our opinion, if you only want to see and visit one such place during your trip, it should be the Blue Lagoon. It is a one-of-a-kind place. You can find more about this rather remarkable resort here: Blue Lagoon – Iceland’s most famous geothermal spa.
* **Try the traditional Icelandic dishes**  
  Traditional Icelandic cuisine can be quite challenging, but it’s impossible to taste it anywhere else in the world, and it leaves an extraordinary impression. You can read all about it in this article: Iceland for Foodies – What’s Worth Trying and Where. It’s really worth experiencing.
* **Excursion to a lava cave**  
  Island owes both its origins and its current appearance in large part to volcanoes. A visit to a lava tunnel (or lava cave, if you prefer) gives a very interesting perspective on this phenomenon. The most interesting of these is the Vidgelmir, but if you’re feeling adventurous and want to save a bit, you can see a similar one not far away, but on your own and for free: Surtshellir.
* **Visit Perlan**  
  When going to Iceland, we are unlikely to think about visiting museums, but Perlan allows you to understand the geology, biology and history of Iceland in a way that is hard to make up “on the road”. It’s worth a visit, especially at the beginning of your trip. You will get more out of seeing volcanoes, glaciers or Icelandic animals in the wild later. More about Perlan: Sightseeing Reykjavik (Perlan).

Unfortunately, the total cost of all these attractions is at least $500 per person (as of 2023). Each of these attractions is really worth the price, but if you must cut costs, see only the free lava cave (Surtshellir), skip the Blue Lagoon (instead, visit one of the free hot springs) and possibly skip a visit to Perlan. The two most interesting and unique attractions – the ice cave tour and the whale watching cruise – are about $300/person in total, and while that’s still a lot, it’s really worth finding the money for.

If  
you don’t want to complete the trip at the absolute lowest possible cost, it’s worth allocating about $500 per person for some of the most interesting attractions. This will make your trip to Iceland much more complete – you will get to know it much better.

### Additional attractions

If you want to use paid tours, the offer is extremely wide and you can actually spend as much as you want.

Here are just a few popular extras:

* a trip to the volcano chamber Þríhnúkagígur costs approx. $315;
* snorkeling in Silfra: about $90 (diving: $170),
* glacier hike: about $150,
* trips to both ice caves (Katla and Jokulsarlon): 2 x $170,
* visit to other hot lagoons and spa centers (Top 10 hot springs and pools of Iceland);
* boat cruise around the bay of Jokulsarlon: $50-100 (depending on boat),
* Museums and exhibitions in Reykjavik (What to see in Reykjavik).

This list could go on for ever… You can book all of these attractions and many more at best prices using our dedicated portal: Rumbomundo – Tourdesk.

All of these activities, tours and attractions are, of course, interesting. Many of them are experiences that can’t be enjoyed anywhere else in the world. If budget (and time) is not an issue for you – by all means take advantage.

## Total costs of a trip to Iceland

As we mentioned before, the final cost is very much determined by the size of your group, season and duration, mode of travel and how early you are ready to make all your reservations.

Obviously, there is no limit to how much one can spend. One night in Lagoon Suite, with private access to a mini-SPA, in Blue Lagoon costs 340,000 kr, which is about 2200 EUR (breakfast included 😀 ). A 3-day stay here with full board and a scenic helicopter tour for 2 people will set you back some 8500 EUR.

As incredible as this sounds, we decided to illustrate the costs of a more down-to-earth trip for 4 people for 7 days. (See the table below.)

The **economy** scenario includes: a small car (such as Kia Rio) for 4 people, sleeping in tents, cooking your own meals, minimum paid activities and early bird bookings (at least 6 months in advance) and/or special deals on all rentals and bookings.

The **comfort** scenario includes: a larger car (such as Kia Ceed wagon), for 4 people; staying in hostels and/or B&Bs, 2-3 meals in affordable restaurants, basic tourist attractions, rather late booking (some 3 in advance) and regular (no discount) prices of flights, accommodation and car rental.

| Total cost of a trip to Iceland for 4 people for 7 days | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | May | | July | |
|  | budget | comfort | budget | comfort |
| car (rental, gas) | $400 | $490 | $820 | $910 |
| full insurance | – not incl. – | $280 | – not incl. – | $280 |
| accommodation | $230 | $1,270 | $230 | $1,900 |
| flights | $640 | $1,180 | $1,000 | $2,090 |
| food | $320 | $640 | $320 | $640 |
| attractions | $230 | $900 | $230 | $900 |
| Total cost (4 pax) | $1,820 | $4,760 | $2,600 | $6720 |
| Cost per person | $455 | $1,190 | $650 | $1,680 |

As you can see, when you want to save money and choose to go out of season, you can go below $500 per person. If you are lucky with plane ticket and car rental prices and if you decide, for instance, not to eat in restaurants, even with this low budget you can still save quite a lot for all sorts of paid attractions. A whale-watching cruise is really worth it!

One the other hand, if you do not make your bookings well in advance; if you are not flexible about your trip dates and you like your comfort or extra attractions, the cost can easily double. Plus, if you want to visit Iceland in summer – it can easily quadruple.

## Other guides

Regardless of how much you spend on your trip, it’s definitely worth ‘squeezing’ the most out of it.

You can find ready-made trip plans that can be easily tailored to your own requirements here:

* Iceland Short Trip Plan: 3 to 5 days
* Spring trip plan to Iceland, in 7 to 13 days
* Best plan to Iceland (summer, 4×4, 14 days)

Plenty of guides, more and less detailed, both on what to see and how to prepare for the trip, have been collected here:

* Iceland Travel Tips

Meanwhile, we’ve compiled an overview of the most interesting places to visit and experiences to have in this article and the next:

* Iceland’s Greatest Attractions [Top 10]

If you only have a few days at your disposal, but want to see as many of Iceland’s amazing attractions as possible – this travel plan is exactly for you.

The basic version of this plan is a 5-day trip. You won’t get around the island in that time, but many of the most important and interesting attractions of Iceland are absolutely within your reach.

You will also find a shortened, 3-day plan below, as well as an extended version – a plan and detailed itinerary for 7 days. If you’re coming for more than 7 days, then proceed to our 7 to 13 days itinerary based on getting around Iceland on famous route 1.

## Top places to see in 5 days in Iceland

On a short trip to Iceland you will focus on visiting the **south, south-west and west** parts of the country. You will stay relatively close to the capital Reykjavik and the international airport in Keflavik, but more importantly: this part of Iceland has lots and lots of attractions packed on a relatively small area. So you can really see a lot in limited time and with limited driving.

The highlights of the 5-day itinerary include the so-called Golden Circle (including the famous Geysir and the continental rift in the Thingvellir National Park), black beaches, several glaciers, Diamond Beach and Jokulsalron Bay, countless waterfalls and volcanoes (including the newest – Litli-Hrutur), lava caves and ice caves (especially if you go in winter), the beautiful Cape Snaefellsnes and any number of hot springs.
