# [43] https://rumbomundo.com/self-catering-in-iceland-all-you-need-to-know

Iceland offers many great restaurants, but if you want to keep your trip budget in check, you’ll need to prepare most of your meals yourself. What are the kitchens we can use in Iceland and what you need to keep in mind when preparing for this type of trip – we want to cover all this in this guide.

In this article:

1. Self-catering and grocery shopping in Iceland
2. Cooking in hostels in Iceland
3. Cooking in mountain hostels in Iceland
4. Cooking at campsites in Iceland
   1. Cooking at campsites in the Iceland’s interior
5. Cooking in an RV in Iceland
6. Cooking on backpacking trips in Iceland
   1. Freeze-dried foods – the perfect innovation
7. Barbecues in Iceland

## Self-catering and grocery shopping in Iceland

Eating out in Iceland is quite expensive. Even in cheaper restaurants, the prices of main courses usually settle somewhere in the neighborhood of $25. In more expensive restaurants, a 6-course dinner menu starts at $125 per person. It’s worthwhile to try the local specialties, but with such price levels, some tourists – from all over the world – need to rely on their own cooking skills. For more on local specialties, unique dishes that are really worth trying, and where to do it and for how much, check out this article: What to eat in Iceland – interesting dishes and prices in restaurants

B  
ear in mind that cooking on your own requires proper organization of the entire trip – accommodation, travel, shopping, but also dishes, cutlery or possibly gas for the stove. We write about this in detail below.

If you cook for yourself, you will also do the shopping yourself. From this side, pay attention not only to the fact that not all supermarket chains are equally cheap, but also to the fact that outside Reykjavik such cheap big grocery stores are not very many at all. So you need to plan your shopping well, especially if you rent a small car for 4 or 5 people and simply can’t fit a week’s worth of provisions into it.

Grocery shopping is also more expensive than in many other countries, but not all products are so expensive that, for example, it pays to bring them with you from home. We write about how much food costs in Icelandic stores, which supermarkets are the cheapest and what you can bring with you to Iceland in this article: Shopping in Iceland: food prices and grocery store opening hours

C  
ar rental companies, hostels and campgrounds – especially those in and near Reykjavik (Keflavik, Grundavik) – often operate a **free exchange shelf**. Tourists who are leaving the island can leave things there that they won’t take with them on the plane, and those who have just arrived can take these things completely free of charge. Very often you can find some coffee, tea, sugar, gas bottles for tourist stoves, maps, guidebooks, flashlights and many more there… Use it without restraint, but on the other hand, when you’re leaving the country, leave things you won’t need on a similar shelf in the last place where you stay overnight.

## Cooking in hostels in Iceland

If you’re staying in hostels, you’ll have access to a pretty well-equipped kitchen and dining area. Usually you will also find small quantities of various products left behind, by other tourists. Usually it is, for example, salt, some pasta and/or rice, sometimes jam, coffee, tea, etc. Also, you’ll use the refrigerator without a problem, although you’ll probably keep most of your food in your car, since you rarely sleep twice in one place, and the nights are cool practically all year round.

Between hostels you’ll probably travel by car, so buying and carrying heavier items – cans, jars, etc – won’t be a problem either. This is certainly a very convenient solution and – for Iceland – quite inexpensive.

In those private guesthouses where guests are provided with a shared kitchen, the situation is the same.

In a hostel kitchen you have to fit in (or pass) with other guests, but you cook practically like at home. For your use you have a comfortable kitchen, all pans, kettles, dishes, cutlery, shelves, cloths, etc… Things usually have to be washed up after yourself, but there is always hot water, so this is also not a problem.

In the afternoon and evening, individual groups or people often cook at different times, so there is little problem with ‘passing’ each other in the kitchen. It can be more difficult in the mornings, but we have never encountered any serious problems due to an excess of people in the kitchen.

## Cooking in mountain hostels in Iceland

Things are a little different if you want to sleep and cook in mountain refuges. These are very diverse facilities and it’s best to see each one carefully before booking or…. be prepared for anything.

Some hostels (e.g. Kerlingarfjoll) provide campers with a well-equipped, brick and heated kitchen with a dining area. In others (e.g. Nyidalur), the kitchen is made available to tourists, but is small and less well-equipped. Unfortunately, it’s also often the case that inside the hostel building you can only eat dishes bought from the hostel restaurant (Hveravellir, Laugarfell), and if you want to cook something of your own, you have to do it outside (sic!), with your own equipment.

Finally, the smallest shelters (like Fimmvorduhals) are basically small and very simple mountain shelters. They don’t have a separate kitchen or dining room at all, and being there, you have to use common sense. If the weather is nice, cook outside. If it’s ugly, get along with the other guests on how you’ll solve it….

Only in the largest hostels can you leave your garbage. In the others – garbage you take with you. Hot water and some place to wash up is probably in each of them, but often outside. Well, and washing up liquid or cloth you must have your own. So have that in mind as well.

## Cooking at campsites in Iceland

There are plenty of campsites in Iceland, and it’s easy to stay overnight (at least from May to September – when all of them are open). However, cooking at campsites has different requirements. Particularly important here is the distinction between campsites in the interiors (usually based on some kind of hostel) and outside the interiors. At campsites outside the interiors (especially those along Highway 1) some kind of canteen and kitchen you will almost always find (yes: not always, but almost always). Unfortunately, they will rarely be spacious, warm and well-equipped rooms.

Positive standouts here include the campground in Grundavik, Camping 66.12 North in Manarbakki in the far north, or the campsites in Fludir and Thorisstadir. They provide camping guests with sufficiently spacious, not badly equipped and protected from the cold and wind kitchen-canteens. On the other hand, the most common standard in Iceland (also on Road 1!) is a brick and equipped, but really small kitchen. You’ll be able to prepare everything in it fairly comfortably, but sometimes you’ll have to wait for the previous guests to finish cooking and free up space.

Unfortunately, at some campsites – including those outside the interiors – the standard is really low. For example, in Grundarfjordur there is no kitchen or canteen for guests at all. At Camping Myvatn there is only a rather flimsy shed with tables, but no kitchen for cooking, and at Lifsmotun campground, for example, there is a kitchen, but inside the wind is blowing and the temperature is basically the same as outside.

U  
se the campground kitchen as often as you can, but be prepared to be fully self-reliant and independent.

### Cooking at campsites in the Iceland’s interior

Cooking at campsites in the interior also varies, although here the proportions are reversed, so to speak. These campsites most often do NOT provide any kitchen for guests, and the canteen offers a place to sit, but rarely really protects from the wind or cold. An example is probably the largest and most popular campsite in the interior – Landmannalaugar, where the common canteen is a large, but cold, airy, yet heavily crowded military-garden type tent.

At campsites that operate next to the hostel, you can sometimes use the hostel and cook something on your own stove inside the building. However, for example, campsites in Landmannahellir or Hveravellir do not provide campers with any facilities. On the other hand, Basar Hut, for example, provides campers with a special separate shelter, but the shelter itself cannot even be entered by people who do not stay there overnight. A complete, and very very positive exception, is the aforementioned Kerflingarfjoll campground, where, in a separate brick and heated building, campers have at their disposal not only a canteen, but also several large cooking burners and virtually all the necessary kitchen equipment, sinks, trash cans, hot water, etc.

R  
emember that the wind is really strong in Iceland almost constantly. If you want to cook on your own at campsites, you not only need to take care of your own stove and an adequate supply of gas bottles (jetboil here really “does the job”). Be prepared that, because of the strong wind, you will often cook in your tent’s entry or inside your camper (it might be tricky in the small ones). Alternatively – do investigate the campsite’s kitchen before you decide to stay there for the night.

## Cooking in an RV in Iceland

Of course, among camping guests, those who came in an RV have it best. Especially in the larger ones – motorhomes – a comfortable kitchen and table are always at your disposal regardless of the temperature, wind or crowd outside. This is important, because this way you can also cook without any problems in the middle of the day, somewhere by a beautiful waterfall or a charming canyon… Just remember not to pour out dirty water or leftovers in forbidden places. Some campers – such as off-road, 4×4 ones – have a kitchen sink, but without a tank for so-called gray water. The water from the sink then lands directly on the grass or asphalt under the car – don’t do this outside the campground, and stay sensible at the campground as well….

If you are moving in a smaller camper – campervan, it will be more convenient to cook outside the car. If necessary, you can always do it inside as well. Given the strong wind and frequent low temperatures, you can cook inside the camper quite often….

Whether it’s a campervan or motorhome, a stove and some gas supply will definitely get you one along with the car. You can buy cartridges for small stoves at many markets and most gas stations (those with any store, of course), as well as at some campgrounds. On the other hand, you will replace an empty large cylinder for a full-size cooker only at larger gas stations.

C  
artridges for small stoves can be bought at most markets and gas stations. As for the larger gas cylinders – the ones for RVs and larger campervans, there are a lot of gas stations that can replace them, but the availability of specific types of cylinders varies, and sometimes you won’t get yours at the first station. Don’t wait until both of your cylinders are empty – swap the empty one as soon as possible.

Either way, driving an RV and being able to prepare a meal anytime and anywhere makes it perfectly easy to plan the entire trip and saves a lot of time.

## Cooking on backpacking trips in Iceland

If you’re planning to cook at campgrounds because you’re trekking through Iceland on foot, you probably know how to prepare brilliantly for such a trip (Iceland is hardly a beginner’s terrain). Just keep in mind that most of the hostels in the Icelandic interiors don’t look much like the Polish ones. The possibility of shopping there will be severely limited (the exception is the not badly stocked Landmannalaugar). Similarly, restaurants – if there is one in a hostel at all, it is 99% really expensive – you are unlikely to find dishes for less than 80 PLN.

So, when hiking for a few days (e.g., on Laugavegur), freeze-dried food will work great (it’s best to bring it from Poland). It will be difficult to find freeze-dried food in Iceland, but in almost every market you will find, for example, Chinese soups for about 80 ISK (that’s PLN 2.50), or dishes that require only a short boil – for example, a serving of Italian ravioli with ham (250 g) is about 500 ISK (about PLN 15). Of course, dry pasta, rice, sauces in bags – all this is easily available.

Water on the trails is available practically only in the valleys, and these are deep and very steep. The fresh glacial relief is beautiful, but a bit non-functional. Therefore, carry a lot of bottles with you and fill them at each stream.

### Freeze-dried foods – the perfect innovation

If we want to minimize both the cost of purchasing and transporting food for a slightly longer trip, freeze-dried food, increasingly popular among tourists, are an interesting solution.

Freeze-dried foods are food products that have undergone freeze-drying, or sublimation drying (they are first deep-frozen and then quickly heated in a vacuum, so that the ice crystals sublimate, i.e. turn immediately into water vapor). It is currently the most perfect method of preserving food – mushrooms, vegetables and fruits, meats, and even herbs and cheeses. Thanks to freeze-drying, food retains the physical, biological and chemical properties of natural raw materials and is free of preservatives. And, by the way, it takes up very little space in your suitcase and, put in your backpack, does not overload it like canned food. It is estimated that most retain no more than 6%-10% of their original weight. To prepare a wholesome and reasonably tasty meal, all you need to do is top up the contents of the package with water and heat. Comparisons to the instant noodle soups are very unfair to freeze-dried food, both in terms of quality, variety of flavors and nutritional values. Although the preparation of the dish itself looks similar, it is really a completely different world, and freeze-dried food is used not only on all professional high-mountain expeditions, but also by NASA in space…

The dried foods work well primarily as a relatively quick warm meal during the day, when you really need to reduce every pound in your backpack, and you won’t be at the store for several days. It’s not a bad idea to take freeze-dried food as an emergency meal in case something goes wrong and your march is delayed a couple of hours or a full day from your plan. When assumptions fail, we have overestimated the possibilities, the weather or the river does not allow us to go faster, or we have spent too much time in some particularly beautiful place, a supply of freeze-dried food protects us at least in terms of food. Freeze-dried food is a good, light and nonperishable idea for such a quick lunch or emergency dinner.

The best places to buy freeze-dried food are online and stationary stores that offer an assortment for travelers. Well, and it’s definitely worth doing it while you’re still in Poland, before you leave, because they’re hard to buy in Iceland. Lyofood brand meals are probably the tastiest. The largest portions are offered by Trek’n eat. And the best value for money in terms of quality and taste is probably Summit to Eat.

You can find a wide selection of dishes on Amazon, among others: LyoFood on Amazon

C  
onsidering Icelandic prices and weather conditions (especially if you plan to travel on foot in the interior), taking a supply of freeze-dried food with you makes a lot of sense. Note: if you like to eat a lot – buy two-person meals. Even those are not that large…

## Barbecues in Iceland

Although the nights in Iceland are almost always cold and the wind almost never stops, especially in summer, the beautiful evenings are very long, so barbecues are quite popular at the campsites. Barbecue pitches are located at quite a few campsites and are usually provided to guests at no charge. You can then buy coal and firelighters at the camp store or from the campground staff, but of course it is cheaper to buy them at almost any market or gas station store.

If you’re renting a car or campervan to drive around Iceland, perhaps it’s worth renting a small, foldable, tourist barbecue along with it as well? Many car rental companies offer this option and the taste of a grilled steak or trout somewhere in the wild interiors is absolutely unforgettable.

If you are using your own barbecue, ask the campground staff if there are designated areas for this, and possibly make arrangements with your neighbors if they will not be disturbed.

Of course, meats for the barbecue – lamb, poultry, fish and vegetables – are available in a wide selection in virtually every market, both in already seasoned form and completely raw.

Carrying coal and firelighters with you, as well as raw meat, complicates the logistics somewhat. The grilling itself is also not the fastest, and forces you to sit outside regardless of the weather. But then, after a few days of eating instant noodles, hot dogs and dried foods, a lamb steak, fish or fresh-grilled zucchini is an attraction worth any sacrifice.

# [44] https://rumbomundo.com/renting-a-car-in-iceland-a-complete-guide

Renting the right car to explore Iceland is certainly one of the most important decisions affecting both the cost and overall shape of the trip, and ultimately our satisfaction with it. So in this article we answer questions about whether you need to rent a car in Iceland, how to do it, what the alternatives are, how much it costs, and what to look for when renting a car in Iceland.

In this article:

1. Is it necessary to rent a car in Iceland
2. How much does it cost to rent a car in Iceland
   1. How much does it cost to rent a car in Iceland at different times of the year
   2. Is it better to rent a car in Iceland well in advance or at the last minute
   3. How to reduce the cost of car rental and accommodation in Iceland
3. Is it worth buying full car insurance in Iceland?
4. Is it worth it to rent a 4×4 car in Iceland?
5. Where is the best place to rent a car in Iceland
   1. The best search engines for renting a car in Iceland
   2. Reputable car rental companies in Iceland
6. Common questions about car rental in Iceland
   1. Is it possible to rent a car in Iceland without a credit card?
   2. Is it possible to rent a car in Iceland without being 21 years old?
   3. Is a Polish driver’s license enough in Iceland?
   4. Is it possible to pick up a car at Reykjavik airport?
   5. I arrive in Iceland late at night – can I pick up my car then?
   6. Do cars in Iceland have winter tires?
7. Other tips on driving in Iceland

## Is it necessary to rent a car in Iceland

The short answer to this question is: yes, you have to. The slightly longer answer, on the other hand, is: well, you don’t have to, but it’s better to do it nonetheless.

![schemat Islandii z drogą nr 1, interiorem i złotym kręgiem](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Islandia-interior1-450-2.png)Iceland is a fairly oval-shaped island with an interior accessible only in summer, and most of the (easily accessible) attractions are located on the coasts, along the popular road no. 1 called the Þjóðvegur 1, Hringvegur or simply: the ring road.

Hence, a typical trip to Iceland (see, for example.: Around Iceland – a 7 to 13-day Itinerary) is based precisely on going around the island all the way on road No. 1. If we have more time, we can add to the plan especially visiting the Snaefellsnes peninsula north of Reykjavik, the Westfjords peninsula on the northwestern edge of the island, and finally the northern and northeastern coasts. And if you’re coming in the summer, it’s a must to see at least parts of the interior.

And all of these excursions are best accomplished just by renting a car yourself.

However, if you want to avoid renting and/or driving yourself, or if you want to explore Iceland by bike or on foot at all – read our tips here: Sightseeing in Iceland without a car.

On the other hand, if you are considering renting an RV and are looking for a comparison of the costs of a car and RV trip, you will find this information in the following article: Renting an RV in Iceland – a Complete Guide.

## How much does it cost to rent a car in Iceland

The lowest rental price we were able to find in Iceland for a tiny car in the off-season is USD 110 for 5 days, or about $22 per day. However, renting a large car in the summer (in high season) involves a cost up to 10 times higher, as much as approx. $1,000 for 5 days! So it is difficult to give a clear answer to the question of how much it costs – it depends.

Theprice of renting a car depends much **less** on what kind of car it is, and much **more** on what month you rent it for and how far in advance.

Renting even the largest car in the off-season costs less than renting the smallest car, but in the summer – during the peak season. Similarly, often renting even a large car, but at the right time (usually: at the last minute), can cost less than renting a small car, but when prices are high in general.

All of this is based on a survey of car rental prices in Iceland, which we have been conducting since the beginning of 2023. Data from these surveys, in the form of charts, are presented below.

### How much it costs to rent a car in Iceland at different times of the year

The biggest impact on the cost of renting a car in Iceland is **when you rent the car for**, or more precisely: whether you rent it for the summer or for another season.

The average prices of renting each popular type of car, depending on **the month you rent it for**, are as follows:

| Car rental costs in Iceland, for 5 days, depending on the month FOR WHEN we rent | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | small (e.g., Kia Picanto) | medium (e.g. Hyundai i30) | large (e.g., Skoda Octavia) | medium 4×4 (e.g., Dacia Duster) | larger 4×4 (e.g., Toyota RAV4) |
| March | $180 | $220 | $270 | $230 | $275 |
| May | $160 | $210 | $230 | $215 | $260 |
| July | $340 | $370 | $445 | $450 | $500 |
| October | $135 | $165 | $190 | $205 | $215 |
| December | $180 | $230 | $240 | $240 | $270 |

Real car rental costs in Iceland  
source: own data for 2023-2025

Thegraphs below show a complete overview of how the prices of a particular model change over time. On the other hand, in all tables (including the one above), lists and comparisons, we use neither the lowest nor the highest, nor even the average prices, as they could be misleading. **Rather, we show typical low prices** instead. These are average prices, but from those periods when a particular model or type of car was relatively cheap. So these are low prices, but nevertheless realistically possible to ‘hunt down’. At the same time, each of these models can be rented even cheaper, as long as you have enough luck or patience.

As you can see, rental prices for the second half of the year (October, December) are about 10% lower than for the first half (March, May), but the differences pale in comparison to summer. You can clearly see from the table that car rental prices for summer (represented by July) are usually about twice as high as rental prices for the same cars for any other time of the year.

Note that – as we wrote earlier – even renting a sizable SUV, such as a Toyota RAV4 or Mitsubishi Eclipse Cross **in the off-season** costs less (about USD 325-350 for 5 days) than renting a tiny Kia Picanto in the summer (an average of USD 440 for 5 days).

Perhaps a better illustration for this are the charts for individual models. See how rental prices for a popular model – like the Dacia Duster – vary depending on what month you rent the car for and WHEN you rent it:

![Chart: Cost of renting Dacia Duster cars for 5 days in selected months, depending on the date of booking](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Duster-months-rumbomundo-705x436.gif)

Chart: Cost of renting Dacia Duster cars  
for 5 days in selected months, depending on the date of booking  
source: own data and compilation

The chart clearly shows that, although the rental prices for March, May, October and December “wave” throughout the year, the rental prices for July are always much higher than them. It also looks quite similar for other types or classes of cars:

![Chart: price of renting a small car for 5 days in Iceland (all seasons, selected months)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Aygo-months-rumbomundo-225x150.gif)Toyota Aygo

![Chart: price of renting a medium-sized car for 5 days in Iceland (all seasons, selected months)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/MazdaCX30-months-rumbomundo-225x150.gif)Mazda CX-30

![Chart: price of renting a compact car for 5 days in Iceland (all seasons, selected months)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Skoda-months-rumbomundo-225x150.gif)Skoda Octavia

![Chart: price of renting a regular 4x4 car for 5 days in Iceland (all seasons, selected months)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/RAV4-months-rumbomundo-225x150.gif)Toyota RAV4

Thecharts show that – especially for July – the moment WHEN you rent your car is also of colossal importance. Prices do change A LOT over time. We write about this in more detail later in the article.

Of course, even larger cars are also available for rent – in particular: really big, off-road SUVs (with Toyota Land Cruiser at the forefront) and 7-9 passenger vans. We don’t research their prices that closely, because these cars are very expensive, less popular and a bit niche even. However, the search engines we recommend also show the prices of those models.

Renting a 9-passenger bus (watch out for luggage!) or a large SUV (such as a Mitsubishi Pajero or Toyota Land Cruiser) in low season costs about USD 750 – 875 for 5 days, and in high season, in summer: about USD 1,375 – 1,625 for 5 days.

**When are the lowest car rental prices in Iceland?**  
For each type of car, the cheapest month to rent it in Iceland is October, although rental prices in November and December are similarly low. During this period, we can rent the smallest cars (on average!) for as little as about 175 dollars for 5 days, and only the largest 4×4 SUVs cost more than $250 for 5 days of rental.

**When are the highest car rental prices in Iceland?**  
For each type of car, the most expensive month of its rental in Iceland is July. These high prices appear already in the second half of June and usually last until the end of August. During this period (on average!) even the smallest cars cost more than $375 (for 5 days) and rental prices for large SUVs approach even $750 (for 5 days).

### Is it better to rent a car in Iceland well in advance or at the last minute

Of course, the **average prices** we’ve shown above are only part of the whole picture. The prices for renting individual models do change a lot throughout the year, even if you don’t change the month **for which** you want to rent it.

The chart below shows how the rental prices for selected models have been changing for the past three years:

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for July (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-JULY-rumbomundo-705x429.gif)

Chart: Car rental prices in Iceland in July, depending on the week when you book

Note that in both 2023 and 2024, rental prices for all (surveyed) types of cars fell the closer you got to July and **were lowest in June**.

For example, for renting a popular Dacia Duster (for 5 days, for July 2024, the red line on the chart) one had to pay more than $600 for almost the entire period from October ’23, until the beginning of April ’24. But those who waited until the last minute could rent the same Dacia for as low as $375 by June 2024! That’s almost half the price!

InJune 2024, you could rent any car for 5 days in July that same year, for under $440. Meanwhile, you had to pay at least $500 for the same period even for the smallest Toyota Aygo (or similar model) if you wanted to rent it much in advance – back in late 2023.

Importantly: the prices for July 2023, while higher overall, behaved similarly. That is, they also began to fall sharply around May and were lowest in June. It seems that one can conclude that this is typical behavior and that **car rental prices for July in Iceland are lowest at the last minute** – only about a month in advance.

Prices for summer 2025 were already quite low at the end of 2024 (see chart above). It is to be expected that these prices will rise in the spring, but are likely to return to these lows again in May-June, or perhaps even fall lower still.

For other seasons (and months surveyed), prices do not change as much. You cannot see such a clear downward trend the closer you get to the time of rental. Nonetheless, even there you can see changes of up to 50%, although since these prices are generally lower, the 50% decreases are also of lesser nominal value.

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for March (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-March-rumbomundo-480x292.gif)March

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for May (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-May-rumbomundo-480x292.gif)May

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for October (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-October-rumbomundo-480x284.gif)October

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for December (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-December-rumbomundo-480x292.gif)December

So let’s go back to the original question: how early should you book/rent a car for a trip to Iceland? Generally speaking, it’s best to do it only about 1 month prior to your trip.

As you can see from the charts above:

* If you are looking for a car for a winter trip (e.g., December or March): you will find the best prices about a month in advance (November and February, respectively);
* If you are looking for a car for a spring trip to Iceland (e.g., in May): the best time to ‘hunt’ for good prices is from the beginning of March, although usually (with exceptions) you’ll the best prices in April;
* You’ll find the best car rental prices for an autumn trip to Iceland in summer – in July and August – so a little earlier than for other seasons – about 2-3 months before your trip;
* And you’ll find the best car rental prices for summer, as we indicated earlier, at the last minute – about a month before your departure;

Ofcourse, it isn’t enough to find a good bargain. You also need to know it when you see it 🙂 That’s why we recommend analyzing the charts shown – if you find the car you need at a price close to the minima in these charts then take it, even if you still have a long time left before you leave.

### How to reduce the cost of a trip to Iceland

Although car rental prices in Iceland are lowest in October, it is not necessarily also the case that the entire trip will be cheapest (let alone best) in October. Leaving aside the flight cost, the total cost of the trip is also greatly influenced by the chosen standard or type of accommodation. And, of course, the “per person” cost is enormously influenced by how many people you are traveling with.

See the table below: a 4-person trip in May, based on driving a Dacia Duster and sleeping in guesthouses, can be cheaper (per person) than a 2-person trip, even if they both sleep in the back of that Dacia (since it can be both cold and wet under a tent in May).

| Cost of car and accommodation for 2-4 people (5 days on site, May 2025) | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 2-person trip | | | 4-person trip | | |
|  | T. Aygo +tent | D. Duster +trunk | campervan +campsites | T. Aygo +hostels | D. Duster +hostels | campervan +campsites |
| car | $160 | $230 | $365 | $160 | $230 | $810 |
| insurance | $185 | $205 | $210 | $185 | $205 | $260 |
| fuel | $275 | $325 | $325 | $275 | $325 | $375 |
| accommo- dation | $190 | $190 | $190 | $1,000 | $1,000 | $385 |
| Total | $810 | $950 | $1,090 | $1,620 | $1,760 | $1,830 |
| Total pp. | $405 | $475 | $545 | $405 | $440 | $460 |

Typical car and accommodation costs for a 5-day trip in May  
source: own data; costs as of 2025.

In the same way, we counted typical costs for 2- and 4-person trips at different times of the year and with different overnight stays. The results may perhaps be surprising to many.

Although July is obviously the most expensive for any type of trip, please note that **a tent trip in July can be cheaper** than a trip with a campervan or sleeping in hostels, at other, cheaper times of the year. See table:

| Total costs in different months (5-day trips, per person costs) | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | T. Aygo +tent (2 people) | D. Duster +tent (4 people) | D. Duster +hostels (4 people) | campervan +campers (2 people) | campervan +campsites (4 persons) | motorhome +campsites (4 people) |
| March | $420 | $285 | $390 | $515 | $430 | $490 |
| May | $405 | $290 | $440 | $545 | $460 | $595 |
| July | $495 | $340 | $745 | $645 | $615 | $780 |
| October | $395 | $280 | $435 | $535 | $430 | $625 |
| December | $415 | $290 | $390 | $525 | $510 | $605 |

Typical car and accommodation costs for a 5-day trip in various months  
source: own data; costs as of 2025.

**Important caveat:** winter tent trips are presented purely for illustration purposes; realistically it is difficult to imagine a situation where this would be a reasonable solution. Even in May or October a tent trip would be very, very demanding.

Typical costs for a tent trip in July are $495 and $340 per person (for a two- and four-person trip, respectively; excluding airfare, food, etc.). Note that it is rather difficult to go below these costs at other times of the year, sleeping in hostels or an RV.

Trunk sleeping only seems like the cheapest solution. After all, apart from all its inconveniences, only 2 people will fit in the trunk, so you will also divide the cost of renting a car, its insurance and fuel by only 2, and not, for example, by 4 people. And this makes a huge difference.

In autumn, spring and winter everyone should rather opt for staying in hotels, guesthouses or hostels. Even campervans, although heated, do not provide a high level of comfort in that time of year (except for the largest and most expensive – motorhomes – maybe), especially since Icelandic “campsites” are often ordinary grassy campgrounds with only the basic sanitary facilities. Campervans work very well from June to September, but in July and August it is cheaper, and almost equally comfortable, to sleep in a tent (you can bring a large one with you, since you’re not carrying it on your back 🙂 ).

We write more about campervans and how the costs of an RV and car trip compare in the article Renting an RV in Iceland – a Complete Guide.

## Is it worth buying full car insurance in Iceland?

Ifyou want to feel at ease, you’ll need to buy full-coverage insurance. Or if you’d rather not pay double for the car, you’ll have to drive around Iceland extra carefully and avoid sheep and storms.

![Car insurance cost in Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/sample-insurance.jpeg)

Insurance can almost double your car rental costs in Iceland

Car insurance in Iceland is a bit controversial, because it’s super expensive.

And yes, the cost of possible repairs is quite high, and yes you can find yourself in situations you are not familiar with from your everyday, home experience. But the insurance and rental companies prey on tourists’ sense of security and have learned to dictate very high prices for insurance.

**How much does it cost to fully insure a car in Iceland?**  
Typical costs for full insurance are usually about 5,000 – 6,000 ISK or **$35-$45 per day**. Thus, full insurance can even double the cost of renting the car.

![Tabela cen i warunków ubezpieczenia samochodów na Islandii](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/warunki-ubezpieczen-705x381.jpg)

Sample prices and terms of car insurance in Iceland

Moreover, very often even the so-called “full package” is not full at all.

**First:** in principle, no insurance covers the cost of flooding a car as a result of crossing a river or stream.  
**Second:** wind damage (usually: the wind breaking off your car doors) is also never included (but, unfortunately, can happen quite easily).  
**Third:** chassis damage, wheel or rim damage and towing back to a garage are also quite often excluded by individual companies. So you need to be careful when driving, somewhat regardless of your insurance package.

Alltypes of insurance available in Iceland are described in more detail in this article: Car Insurance in Iceland – A Complete Guide.

Iceland has right-hand traffic and laws very similar to those throughout Europe. Traffic on the roads is calm and, except in Reykjavik, very light. Therefore, if you are an experienced European driver and decide **not to buy additional insurance**, you should be mostly concerned and watching out for the following “most popular” insurance incidents in Iceland:

* **door break-off** by wind (already mentioned above); please always park against the wind – with your front to the wind, even if you can’t see any wind at all;
* **windshield damage**, usually by a pebble from under the wheels of car in front of you or, much less frequently, a car coming from the opposite direction; this can happen also on the tarmac roads, so keep your distance;
* **collision with a sheep**, usually one standing behind a “blind top”; even worse: some drivers don’t want to hurt the animal so much, that they drive off the road, which then sometimes leads to totalling the car; just slow down when you see a blind top road sign;
* nicks, scratches and other typical **parking damage**; these are not common, but all the same hard to avoid; try parking a little further away from where everyone crowds and you should be fine;
* **severe storms** and other weather hazards; yes, the top storms can blow a car right off the road, but they are announced in advance on vedur.is; be ready to pause your trip if a red alert is announced in a region you are in or are heading to;

![rozbite auto na poboczu drogi na Islandii](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/IMG_6490-wymuszenie-350x233.jpg)

Small accident at Skaftafell

Of course, there are also “ordinary” car crashes in Iceland. Speeding, failure to yield or texting while driving tend to bring very similar results in Iceland, as they do around the world. So be careful, as always when driving.

**If you’re coming from the USA**, please remember **priority to the right** is the basic rule for uncontrolled intersections in all of Europe. And it doesn’t matter who got to the intersection first.

Ifyou see a stop or yield sign or if there is no signs, but you see cars approaching from your right – **you have to give way**. They will not stop, not even slow down, even if they can see clearly you were there first. You can only enter an intersection after all the cars with priority have cleared it. No two ways about it!

And it is really tricky to switch sides even for the most experienced drivers. So if you’re coming from a **left-hand traffic country**, just be safe and buy the full insurance package, regardless of the inflated costs.

## Is it worth renting a 4×4 car in Iceland?

Yes, as long as you come to Iceland in summer and intend to visit the interior, or you come in winter and intend to go all around the island, it makes all the sense in the world to rent a 4×4 or a 4WD/AWD vehicle. In other cases, a 4-wheel drive will be rather unnecessary.

4-wheel drive cars are very useful and even necessary if you are coming to Iceland in summer (mid-June to mid-September) and intend to enter the interior (see: The most interesting places of the Icelandic interior [Top10]).

When visiting in the summer, it’s definitely worth renting a 4×4 car and seeing at least some of the attractions of the Icelandic interior.

![panorama Landmannalaugar](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/landmannalaugar-panorama-705x164.jpg)

Landmannalaugar panorama

Four-wheel drive cars come in handy in the interior, both because they are good at crossing streams and steep gravel climbs, and because, as generally higher-suspension cars, they are less likely to suffer chassis damage on Icelandic gravel roads. That’s why in summer it’s definitely worth renting a 4×4 car.

![road signs warning against crossing the Krossa river ford in Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/krossa-znaki-480x320.jpg)Krossa ford signs

![an off-road vehicle crossing a mountain river](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Krossa-jeep-IMG_0127-480x320.jpg)Crossing the Krossa

![a car crossing the river ford in Landmannalaugar, Iceland](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Landmannalaugar-brod-480x320.jpg)interior

![campsite entry](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Basar-Hut-entrance-480x320.jpg)campsite entry

In contrast, outside the summer season the usefulness of a two-axle drive is rather negligible. In winter, of course, it can sometimes be very helpful for climbing hills (if/when they are snowy or icy), but in southwest Iceland we very rarely encounter conditions in which a 4×4 car can cope and a 2×4 car can not. This is mainly because there are simply no such steep climbs here.

And when a heavy snowstorm strikes, the roads are closed for all traffic until the snow is cleared, so again it doesn’t matter much if your car is a two-wheel drive or a four-wheel drive.

![piękna islandzka zima](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/IMG_4253-zachod-342x148.jpg)

beautiful Icelandic winter

Winter trips (see Winter trip to Iceland – a Complete Guide) are best limited just to the southern coast, the area around Reykjavik and possibly the Snaefellsnes Peninsula.

However, if you still want to go around Iceland in winter, it is indeed worth equipping yourself with a 4×4 car. All-wheel drive can come in handy both in the eastern and western fjords, as well as in the north of the country.

It’sdefinitely worth renting a 4×4 car if you’re coming to Iceland in winter and plan to drive around it. On such a trip in general, you need to be prepared for various, sometimes serious, weather surprises, and a car with four-wheel drive can come in handy on such a trip. If you arrive in winter, but stay in the south and southwest, a 4×4 drive is not necessary.

In contrast, in spring and autumn, there is really no reason to rent a four-wheel drive car.

![Chart: price of renting a car for 5 days in Iceland for May (various types of cars)](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cars-May-rumbomundo-480x292.gif)

The cost of renting different classes of cars for May  
[charts for other months can be found earlier/above in this article]

Another thing to note is that in the off-season, 4WD cars are often just a tad more expensive than 2WD ones. In the chart opposite, see that the cost of renting a 4WD Dacia Duster for May (red line) is often less (sic!) than the cost of a midsize 2WD car (like a Hyundai i30 or Mazda CX-30; purple line), and often even very close to the cost of the smallest 2WD cars – like a Toyota Aygo or Huyndai i10 (green line in the chart).

In such a situation, it’s probably worth opting for the Duster, because although the quality of plastics or electronics in the cabin will probably be worse than in, say, a Mazda, the Duster certainly has a larger trunk and higher suspension. And even if the 4×4 drive itself is unlikely to be useful for anything on a May trip, the larger trunk and higher suspension certainly won’t hurt.

## Where is the best place to rent a car in Iceland

The vicinity of Keflavik Airport is teeming with car rental companies and their huge parking lots with hundreds of cars ready for pickup, so how do you find the best deal in such an expansive market?

Of course, it’s always best to start by analyzing the price charts on RumboMundo 🙂 Here you’ll find key information about what price level is actually attractive for a given car at a given time of year [see charts above]. But the car rental deals themselves are best found on online search engines.

### The best search engines for renting a car in Iceland

The best, fastest and most convenient way to find a great car rental deal in Iceland is to use one of the online search engines. They collate and compare prices (and other terms and conditions) for renting hundreds, if not even thousands, of different types of cars.

In our experience, two of them work best: DiscoverCars.com and ReykjavikCars.com.

* **DiscoverCars.com**  

  ![Discovercars website](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/dicovercars-webpage-361x360.jpeg)

  Discovercars website

  Discover Cars is basically the best comparison site, or search engine, for car rental deals in Iceland that we can recommend.

  It has **the widest selection of** different types of cars, lots of **convenient filters** that allow you to quickly find exactly the car you are looking for and (almost always) **the best prices**. We couldn’t recommend it more.

  Discover Cars almost always offers the best prices on cars in every category. “Almost”, because on some rare occasions we were able to find even better prices on the site we present below – Reykjavik Cars.

  But outside of these two – we can never find better prices anywhere else on the web.

![DiscoverCars.com](//discover-car-hire.postaffiliatepro.com/accounts/default1/bunyh71e/f29909e9.jpg "DiscoverCars.com")![](https://discover-car-hire.postaffiliatepro.com/scripts/iunyh71e?a_aid=RumboMundoCom&a_bid=f29909e9)

* **ReykjavikCars.com**  
  Reykjavik Cars is not as international as Discover Cars. It is focused exclusively on Iceland and Icelandic car rentals. And perhaps that is why sometimes this is where we find the best car rental prices in Iceland.

  ![Przykładowe opcje ubezpieczeń na Reykjavik Cars](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ubezpieczenia-reykjavik-480x237.jpg)

  Sample insurance options at Reykjavik Cars

  An additional distinguishing feature of Reykjavik Cars is certainly the more extensive insurance section. Here, we don’t just have a choice of full insurance (PLATINUM) or none at all (i.e. TPL/CDW alone, which is always included in the price). We can also choose an intermediate option (PREMIUM) – full insurance, but with a deductible.

  It is however best practice to rent a car via a comparison website, but then buy the full insurance package directly from the rental company, as an up-sell. And don’t worry – they will come back to sell it to you. They will send you emails about it and they will try to up-sell it you when you pick-up the car. You’ll have plenty of opportunity.

## Frequently asked questions about car rental in Iceland

Renting a car in Iceland is such an important and expensive thing that it raises many specific questions. We’ve collected them here, for the convenience of everyone reading.

### Is it possible to rent a car in Iceland without a credit card?

Certainly. In practice this “forces” you to buy a full insurance package, but if this is what you are looking for anyhow, you don’t need a credit card for that.

Select “Debit card” and/or “no deposit” in the recommended Discover Cars search engine and you will get the best car rental deals without a deposit and credit card.

### Is it possible to rent a car in Iceland without being 21 years old?

As it is, many companies (though not all) also rent cars in Iceland to people who are under 21 and those who are already 65 or older.

However, most companies require such customers to buy a full insurance package. And insurance for these drivers is usually much more expensive.

You can find many such offers on Discover Cars, which has been recommended here many times. Just enter your true age and country of origin anyway and get offers tailored just for that.

### Do I need an international driving license in Iceland?

No, if you hold a European or US driving licence.  
Yes, if your driving licence was issued in other parts of the world.

### Is it possible to pick up the car at Reykjavik airport?

Yes, although the main, and practically the only international airport in Iceland is the Keflavik airport (KEF), about 50 km away from the capital. This is where planes from all over the world land, and where the vast majority of car rental companies are based. Sometimes – although incorrectly – it is referred to as Keflavik-Reykjavik, but it is still the same airport.

In contrast the **Reykjavik Airport (REK)** is a small municipal airport in the center of Reykjavik. It serves mainly domestic flights and a minimal number of international flights – mainly to Greenland. Only a very limited group of rental companies allow you to pick up a car here. These include, for example, Europcar.

### I arrive in Iceland late at night – can I pick up the car then?

Yes, although directly in the arrivals hall there are stands of only a few international chains (such as Avis or Europcar), practically all rental companies operating in Iceland allow you to pick up (and drop off) a car at any time of the day or night.

This is usually done by shuttle buses, which constantly run between the airport arrivals hall and the headquarters of each rental company. Note that this applies to cars, but not to RVs. While RVs can be dropped-off at any time, pickup is (almost) always during office hours.

### Do cars in Iceland have winter tires?

Yes, and in most cases they are not ordinary winter tires, but special, so-called studded tires. Special studs or spikes are embedded in such a tire precisely, which tremendously improves the tire’s grip on snow and ice. As a result, all cars are great at handling icy driveways or holding on icy corners. Unfortunately, these tires also make noticeably louder noise and slightly increase fuel consumption. However, for safe driving in winter conditions they are invaluable.

Video: studded tires in Iceland

## Other tips on driving in Iceland

In summer and winter, the best option – both for reasons of convenience and cost – will be to rent a private car and sleep in hostels and guesthouses, or in a tent in summer. But in the fall and spring (and especially in June and September), RVs work very well in Iceland. They combine convenience, travel flexibility and, let’s say, ‘reasonable’ costs. All about what kind of RVs in Iceland are available, how much it costs to rent them and what to watch out for when doing so we have collected in the article Renting an RV in Iceland – a Complete Guide.

A huge impact on the total cost of renting your vehicle is the scope and cost of its insurance in Iceland. In Iceland we have at our disposal several types of insurance not known in other countries, and also the whole structure of insurance sold to tourists may vary different from what you are accustomed to in your home country. Learn about the structure, ranges and prices of car insurance in Iceland in this article: Car Insurance in Iceland – A Complete Guide.

Before coming to Iceland, it’s definitely worth familiarizing yourself with the specific conditions of Icelandic roads, the specific regulations in force there and – just in case – about the amount of fines for certain traffic offenses. You will read about all this in this article: Road Conditions, Regulations and Fines in Iceland.

If you are wondering how to arrange your trip route and possibly what car to choose for it, read our description of a selection of the most important and interesting roads you may want to drive on. We have collected them here: The Most Important Roads in Iceland.

Of course, we always encourage you to look at our Top10 lists to pick the most interesting places to see. It’s probably worth starting with Top 10 Things You Need to Do in Iceland.

# [45] https://rumbomundo.com/renting-an-rv-in-iceland

In this article:

1. Is it worth renting an RV in Iceland
   1. Renting a car with a tent on the roof
   2. Renting a campervan
   3. 4×4 campervans – a specialty of Iceland
   4. Motorhome campers
2. The best campervan rentals in Iceland
3. Other guides about driving in Iceland

## Is it worth renting an RV in Iceland

In Iceland you will find plenty of different types of RVs. When looking at their different types, let’s keep in mind the fundamental differences between them. Heating for the sleeping area, a kitchen with a large burner, sink and refrigerator, and a functional bathroom are the basic features with which different types of RVs differ. Of course, the larger ones also offer space to spend time comfortably, while the smaller ones admittedly allow you to sleep inside, but cooking or evening chats are more likely to have to be moved outside or to the camper’s kitchen.

Kamps are great in Iceland especially in late spring. In May and June, the day is already long, campsites are open, roads are passable, and nights are not as cold. At the same time, the cost of renting an RV is still quite reasonable then. A June trip in an RV is a relatively comfortable and inexpensive idea for Iceland.

We describe the advantages and disadvantages of each type of RV later in the text, and here let’s group them just for clarity:

* Motorhomes  
  are the largest vehicles, equipped with both a kitchen and a bathroom, hot water, a refrigerator, plenty of lights and outlets, as well as large beds and plenty of space for both passengers and luggage; 6-person versions are the most popular, but you can find both smaller and larger ones; if someone simply says ‘camper’ they usually mean just motorhome – it’s actually a house on wheels;
* 4×4 motorhomes  
  are usually large semi-trucks (e.g., a Dodge Ram) with something like a small caravan perched on the ‘float’; they are much smaller than motorhomes and not equipped with a bathroom, but are nevertheless more spacious than most campervans, have a sizable kitchen and refrigerator, allow you to stand inside, and, well, are great for driving in the interiors;
* Campervans  
  are usually cars adapted from delivery vans, but you can also find off-road vehicles converted into such campers; they offer the possibility of sleeping inside (and therefore warm), good protection from the wind and (usually) parking heating for cold nights; they usually also have a small refrigerator; however, they do not have a bathroom, and the kitchen is a slightly larger (or quite ordinary) touring burner, which is rather difficult to use inside the car, especially in the smallest models;
* Tent on the roof  
  RVs with a tent on the roof are counted as campers in Iceland basically only because they are rented together with all the camping equipment – stove, dishes, cutlery, chairs, etc.; but, for example, a tourist refrigerator is a rarity in them; the advantage over carrying an ordinary tent is the ease and speed of setting up the rooftop version; certainly the disadvantage is that there is only one tent, so the car is a two-person proposition;

In the following text, we will discuss these in more detail in reverse order – from the simplest cars with a tent on the roof, to full motorhomes.

### Renting a car with a tent on the roof

The primary reason why ordinary cars with a tent on the roof are presented as motorhomes in Iceland is that they are rented together with basic camping equipment. If you want to sleep in tents on the ground, in practice you have to bring them with you, as well as a stove, dishes, cutlery and anything else you want to have with you while camping. However, in such an RV with a tent on the roof, this is already included in the rental price

![samochód z namiotem na dachu stojący na kempingu](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/kamper-namiot-480x270.jpg)

A typical Dacia Duster with a roof tent.

A tent on the roof folds and unfolds faster and easier than one on the ground, but it is only one small “double”. The tent is not heated, and there is practically never a refrigerator on the equipment of such a campervan.Compared to small two-person campervans here we have a lot of luggage space at our disposal, and we do not have to rearrange or hide all the luggage every day when we want to go to bed. In practice, this is quite a considerable convenience. However, the lack of heating in the sleeping area is, in turn, a high price for this convenience. Of course, rental companies will provide us with such a car at any time of the year, but in Iceland in an unheated tent even in summer it can be cold. Therefore, for most tourists this is an interesting option only for the summer months – from June to August. Accommodation in campgrounds allows us to save a lot of money, and at the same time provides the utmost flexibility – we can change the exact itinerary depending on the current situation.

| The cost of renting an RV with a tent on the roof (14 days) | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Dacia Duster | Suzuki Jimny |
| April | 200,000 ISK (approx. 6,200 PLN) | 2,300 EUR (approx. 10,500 PLN) |
| June | 225,000 ISK (approx. 7,000 PLN) | 2500 EUR  (approx. 11,500 PLN) |
| July | 265,000 ISK (approx. 8,200 PLN) | 4500 EUR (approx. PLN 20,700) |

As you can see, the Suzuki Jimny is a much more expensive option, despite being a smaller car. At the same time, it also gets much more expensive in the summer. In this category, the Dacia is certainly a better choice. However, it is worth noting that for a 4- or 5-person trip, renting a suitable campervan may not be more expensive at all, and will certainly provide more comfort (well, and 5-person trips are usually much more fun 🙂 ).

### Renting a campervan

Campervans, true to their name, are usually created from the conversion of a classic van (that is, a van precisely). The rear part of the car is adapted into a bedroom, which can usually also be converted into a seating and cooking area for the day.

![Campervany na kempingu na Islandii](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/kampervany-480x256.jpg)

Popular campervan sizes

You can also find an ordinary passenger car or off-roader – a Dacia Duster, Subaru Forester, Mitsubishi Pajero or even a Land Rover Defender – with the rear cabin and trunk converted into a bedroom for two.

Driving characteristics here, of course, remain the same as in the base car, while cooking and sleeping conditions are spartan, but sufficient. Cooking is almost always in such a car based on a small touring stove powered by gas cartridges (round and oblong, shaped somewhat like spray air fresheners). The stove usually has one burner, but for some cars we get (or can rent) two stoves. So the cooking possibilities are only slightly better than in typical tent conditions. Besides, cooking inside the RV causes it to fog up very quickly, and opening the door unfortunately lets the cold in from outside.

Smallercampervans are usually NOT equipped with a refrigerator. The larger ones usually have a refrigerator, but one that only works while driving and lacks a freezer. Take this into account when deciding on this solution.

In addition, there really is very little space in the campervan in the back, so to a large extent you have to think of it as a tent on wheels rather than a riding house. The most convenient way would be to set up a table and chairs in front of the campervan and cook and eat there, but due to the strong and very frequent Icelandic winds, this is also conspicuously difficult. Nevertheless, since you have to stay at the campsite for the night anyway, we can move the cooking (usually) to the camping canteen and at least the problem of limited kitchen space disappears.

Th e sleeping area of the campervan doesn’t offer much space, but you can certainly get a good night’s sleep. Of course, again, it is more of a standard similar to a tent than even a hostel bed. However, unlike a tent, here we have hard walls to protect us from the wind and heating – both make a huge difference even in summer. In practice, this means that it is a very functional solution also for spring or autumn trips – when there are fewer tourists in Iceland and all prices are noticeably lower.

Naturally, in such a car there is not even the simplest bathroom, let alone a shower. Of course, bathrooms and showers are available at every campsite, but not always in the price of accommodation (although they are never expensive). Renting a campervan will always be more expensive than a 4×4 car, but having our own bedroom saves the cost of guesthouses and we do not have to worry about booking accommodation. The floor we sleep on is always level, well, and we are well protected from the wind and cold. So it is certainly more comfortable than, for example, Duster with a tent.

| Costs of renting a campervan (14 days) | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Citroen Berlingo (2 persons). | Dacia Duster 4×4 (2 persons). | Mitsubishi Pajero 4×4 (2 persons). | Renault Master (5 persons, refrigerator and sink) |
| April | EUR 1450 (approx. PLN 6,700) | EUR 2,300 (approx. PLN 10,600) | 2800 EUR (approx. 12,900 PLN) | 2650 EUR (approx. 12,200 PLN) |
| June | 1450 EUR (approx. 6,700 PLN) | 2750 EUR (approx. 12,700 PLN) | 3200 EUR (approx. 14,700 PLN) | 2800 EUR (approx. PLN 12,900) |
| July | 1700 EUR (approx. 7,800 PLN) | 3650 EUR (approx. 16,800 PLN) | 4750 EUR (approx. 21,800 PLN) | 4500 EUR (approx. 20,700 PLN) |

As you can see from the table above, the smallest campervan is not only clearly cheaper than the others, but also by far the least expensive in summer. The prices of the other 3 models are relatively close to each other, which certainly makes renting the Master, on a per-person basis, the cheapest, but it is a front-wheel-drive car, which makes the comparison to the Pajero or Duster somewhat unfair.

W henrenting a Dacia Duster in campervan version (with a bedroom inside the car) is, as you can see, quite a bit more expensive than the same car with a tent on the roof. It is colder in the tent, of course, but for the difference in price you can buy two really very good sleeping bags….

### 4×4 campers – a specialty of Iceland

Particularly noteworthy is the hybrid created by embedding a kind of small caravan on the back of a large off-road semi-truck (pick-up truck). It’s hard to describe it more clearly – see what it’s about in the photo below

![Camper 4x4 w Thorsmork, Islandia](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/camper-w-thorsmork.jpg)

4×4 camper in Thorsmork

Such a camper is a compromise between an off-road 4×4 and a motorhome. It can also be found in other parts of the world, but it is in the specific Icelandic conditions that it offers some unquestionable advantages. First of all, in such a camper, as in a motorhome, we have a kitchen at our disposal. It is smaller and usually less well equipped than the one in the motorhome, but it is there nonetheless. We have a sizable sink, a constantly running refrigerator with a freezer, large, convenient cabinets. The sizable refrigerator, water heater and heating of the living area are powered by a gas cylinder, which makes the trip very comfortable, even if we can’t connect to the motorhome’s electricity. On the other hand, just like in a campervan, there is neither a toilet nor a shower.

In the living area, there is as much space as in the largest campervans (for example, you can easily stand), but of course, compared to a motorhome, it is still quite claustrophobic. The cab, on the other hand, is made to American 6-passenger standard, so there is plenty of space here. However, unlike both those types of campervans, here we can’t walk down the middle from the cab to the living area. Every time you have to get out and enter the other part from the back. This is not a big problem, but a certain inconvenience as much as possible. On the other hand, where such a 4×4 camper shines is driving on mountain roads. The Dodge Ram 1500 (or similar) semi-trucks on which these campers are based offer more than 300 horsepower, 4-wheel drive, of course, a locking differential and a reducer. Plus really big, tall wheels, well, and an equally tall, off-road suspension. So this is as full-blooded off-road car as possible. These cars look bizarre, but off-road they perform perfectly. You can drive them practically anywhere in the interior without any problems (the only exception is the Kross, but the brave will not be frightened) and cook food and sleep in relative comfort – lower than in a motorhome or hostel, but still incomparably higher than in a campervan or tent. In addition, it is a 4-person car, so it can be cheaper per person than campervans based on typical off-road cars – such as the Toyota Land Cruiser.

Trudely say that a 4×4 campervan is a compromise between an off-road vehicle and a campervan. Rather, it is a combination of the best features of both types of cars.

The disadvantage of such a car is high fuel consumption. The large front and side surfaces cause huge air resistance; on top of that, the really high weight and the usual American automatic transmission, mean that in off-road driving a combustion of 20 l/100 km is not unusual…. The high sides on each side also mean a fair amount of sensitivity to wind gusts, but nevertheless the high unladen weight means that the driver does feel the gusts on the steering wheel, but they don’t throw the car on the road the way they can in a motorhome. Bottom line: for 4 people this is a very, very interesting option. If you want to see the interior, well, and are willing to pay more in exchange for extra comfort (compared to a campervan or sleeping in a tent), then definitely consider such a 4×4 camper.

| The cost of renting a 4×4 camper (14 days) | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Toyota HiLux (3 persons). | Dodge RAM (4 persons) |
| May | 2800 EUR (approx. 12,900 PLN) | 4150 EUR (approx. 19,100 PLN) |
| June | 3300 EUR (approx. 15,200 PLN) | 4250 EUR (approx. 19,600 PLN) |
| July | 4950 EUR (approx. 22,800 PLN) | 6850 EUR (approx. 31,500 PLN) |
4×4 campers have been available since May.

As you can see from the table, 4×4 campers are rather an expensive option. Although per person (assuming full ‘occupancy’) they are even cheaper than the aforementioned Pajero or Land Cruiser, they are up to twice as expensive ‘per person’ compared to the Duster with a tent on the roof. Of course, they perform much better (than the Duster and other cars in this class) off-road and can simply handle a lot more rivers, in a much wider range of conditions. They also certainly provide greater driving, cooking and sleeping comfort, but still, the price for that comfort is high. As you will see in the next table, for the price of a Dodge Ram, you can even rent a luxury 6-passenger motorhome. You won’t drive such a car down the gravel roads, but the comfort of traveling on Road 1 around the island will be even higher.

### Motorhome campers

![kamper typu motor home](https://rumbomundo.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/motorhome-480x320.jpg)

Modern motorhome camper

Motorhomes are the largest of the vehicles we can rent in Iceland. The basic feature of a motorhome camper is that you will find not only a reasonably spacious and well-equipped kitchen with a refrigerator, sink, oven and several-burner stove, but also a bathroom with a shower and toilet. Campers will also usually have a retractable external roof – an awning, but its usefulness in Icelandic conditions is small due to the almost constant strong wind and the sun not getting too high above the horizon. The comfort of traveling in such a camper is absolutely incomparable to the other options described here. Not only because we have a really comfortable kitchen and a small but functional bathroom, but also because these vehicles provide a comfortable table for eating or, for example, playing cards; many well-lit places for reading; a million storage compartments for everything we might need; many 220V power outlets and, of course, USB, and (usually) a comfortable and rich set of camping furniture.

It really is a home on wheels and provides the best combination of travel comfort and flexibility – after all, we sleep in campsites that we don’t have to book. A spoonful: every 2-3 days, however, it’s worth plugging in. In spring this is not a problem, but in summer we need to find either a campsite that is not very crowded, or book such a place at least a day in advance. After all, we can always find a parking space at a campsite, but a parking space with an electricity approach – not necessarily anymore. The camper, of course, works great without such a connection, but then all 220-volt outlets do not work, so we can not charge larger devices – those that can not be charged from a USB or cigarette lighter socket.

Remember that the nominal number of passengers provides that some people (usually 2) will sleep in the mess – on berths unfolded in place of the table and daybeds. Every day such bedding has to be unfolded and folded again in the morning, well, and the people sleeping in the mess hall are always the last to go to sleep and the first to get up. This is not a particular problem, but nevertheless reduces the comfort of the trip. On the other hand, however, giving up sleeping in the mess hall and renting, for example, a 6-person camper for 4 people is simply quite expensive.

When renting an RV for the full number of people, you also need to keep in mind that you will noticeably run out of water supply and fill the toilet cassette faster. This is not a problem, because we spend our nights at campsites anyway, so we can take care of refilling the water and emptying the toilet, but simply these technicalities will not let us forget about them. Similarly, we need to remember to refill the gas in the cylinder (or rather: replace the gas cylinders). Not every gas station offers this service, so if you have already exhausted one cylinder and are using another – replace the former with a full one at the first opportunity, as soon as possible. Without gas, not only the stove will not work, but probably also the refrigerator and heating, so the matter is serious. From the side of the driving and driving itself, modern motorhomes drive very well and easily. However, it is necessary to remember to correct for their huge size. When maneuvering in parking lots and campgrounds, let’s pay attention not only to the overlapping rear, but also to make sure we don’t snag the roof on something….

Video: maneuvering a motorhome camper.

Naturally, the camper also smokes a lot and is sensitive to wind gusts. Most rental companies also do not allow (and rightly so) to drive these vehicles off paved roads. As a result, the interior is beyond the reach of such an RV, but for a trip on Road 1 (and side roads) it is perfectly suitable.

The motorhome camper is a very convenient solution, perfectly combining the comfort of the trip with great independence and flexibility in its implementation.

| Motorhome camper rental costs (14 days) | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Motorhome 4 pers. | Motorhome 6 pers. Economy | Motorhome 6 pers. Luxury |
| April | 3000 EUR (approx. 13,800 PLN) | 3200 EUR (approx. 14,700 PLN) | 3900 EUR (approx. 18,000 PLN) |
| June | 4180 EUR (approx. 19,200 PLN) | 4500 EUR (approx. PLN 20,700) | 4700 EUR (approx. 21,600 PLN) |
| July | 5950 EUR (approx. 27,400 PLN) | 6250 EUR (approx. 28,800 PLN) | 6550 EUR (approx. 30,100 PLN) |

As you can see from the above table motorhome campers are not cheap. Interestingly, the price difference between the smaller and cheaper one and the largest and most expensive one is relatively small – in summer it does not even exceed 10%. In addition, on a per-passenger basis, the smallest motorhome here clearly comes out as the most expensive. And while these prices are obviously high, on a per-passenger basis, even the large luxury model is as competitive as possible against many of the options indicated earlier. Of course, even on such a per-passenger basis, the motorhome is as much as twice as expensive as a Dacia Duster with a tent on the roof, but the comfort of travel in it is also incomparably higher.

### Campervan rentals in Iceland

Campers – both campervans and motorhomes – are quite popular in Iceland. They allow you to save on the cost of accommodation and give you great elelasticity in planning your route. Not surprisingly, there are many different campervan rental companies with a wide variety of models on offer. However, what may be surprising is that the best rental prices can be found at a completely non-specialized Icelandic campervan. That’s the Motorhome Republic website, originally from New Zealand. It offers RV rentals ranging from the smallest and simplest, two-person models based on a Renault Kangoo or similar, all the way up to the largest and most luxurious motorhome (usually the so-called alcove or semi-tegra). The low prices on this site probably have to be explained by the fact that the site is very popular with customers from the US, a very large and affluent group of tourists. Americans are very fond of traveling in RVs (called RVs there – recreational vehicles) and are eager to take them. And the services operating in the largest markets usually offer the best prices. We checked and compared rental prices for different types and sizes of RVs, and practically always the cheapest was just at Motorhome Republic. And at the same time, this service probably offers the widest range of different types of RVs and they are well described and presented, and the vast majority of options (add-ons and insurance) can be fully self-selected. So we don’t have to match the offer of a single rental company, but can choose exactly the model we are interested in and get just the best deal on it.

Loading search form…

Only when it comes to 4×4 campers, especially the largest ones, a better price is sometimes found on CamperVan Iceland or KuKu Campers (although the latter make their offer available through booking.com).

## Other tips on driving in Iceland

A huge influence on the total cost of renting one car or another in Iceland is the extent and cost of its insurance. In Iceland we have several types of insurance not known in other countries, and also the whole structure of insurance sold to tourists is quite different from what we can buy in Poland, for example. Learn about the structure, ranges and prices of car insurance in Iceland in this article: Car Insurance in Iceland. If you’re going to Iceland, it’s definitely worth getting acquainted with the specific conditions of Icelandic roads, the specific regulations in force there and – just in case – about the amount of fines for certain traffic offenses. You will read about all this in this article: Road conditions, regulations and fines in Iceland. If you are wondering how to arrange your trip route and possibly what car to choose for it, read our description of a selection of the most important and interesting roads you may want to drive on. We have collected them here: The most important roads in Iceland. Of course, we always encourage you to look at our Top10 lists to pick the most interesting places to see. It’s probably worth starting with Iceland’s Greatest Attractions [Top 10].
